The House resumed from Monday, March 29, consideration of Bill C-92, an act to amend the Income Tkx Act, the Canada Pension Plan, the Income Tax Conventions Interpretation Act, the Thx Rebate Discounting Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act and certain related acts, as reported (with amendment) from the Standing Committee on Finance; and Motion No. 1.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to speak on this legislation today.
There is growing concern right across Canada that we are having a problem with the fairness of our tax system. Over the last number of years Liberal and Tory governments have introduced a series of tax loopholes and tax measures that have made it inequitable for people across Canada.
Many of the tax policies that have been brought in over the last 15 years to 20 years have resulted in a dramatic shift of taxation from corporate structure to personal structure. At one time the tax bill in Canada was shared equally between corporations and people, about 50 per cent. Over the last number of years through successive tax measures by Liberal and Tory governments this has now shifted so that the income tax burden is being paid approximately 80 per cent by individuals and only 20 per cent by corporations.
Thx policy has also been largely responsible for the increase in the shifting of financial resources from the middle income people to the very wealthy. This has accelerated particularly since the mid-seventies where increasingly there is a group of rich people at the top, a shrinking middle income group in the middle, and a growing poor at the bottom.
The most recent information shows that the top 10 per cent of earners in the country increased their share of the total income from about 23 per cent to 26 per cent over the last two or three years. The share of total income of the bottom 40 per cent has been steadily declining.
The GST was one tax mechanism that Canadians know is blatantly unfair. It is particularly unfair for working families. A big bite has been taken out of their income to pay for the unfair GST. Now we have the government again stepping forward with a tax measure that will help only a few wealthy families in Canada by extending the 21-year rule on family trusts.
It is very difficult to get exact information on family trusts in Canada because of the privacy provisions of the Income Tax Act. Therefore we do not know a great deal, either on a cumulative basis or on an individual basis, about what is involved in family trusts and what kinds of funds are being held within family trusts.
However there are some people within the industry who have made some very good and solid calculations. It is now estimated that there is over $70 billion held in these kinds of trusts. This is not a large amount as a percentage of the total assets held by persons and unincorporated businesses in Canada, which amounts to about $2.4 trillion. The family trusts are only a small percentage, about 3 per cent.
We do not know very much about individuals but there are examples that have come out through court records. One example is the family trust established by Samuel Bronfman for his daughter in 1969. At that time court documents showed that it was valued at $70 million. It has been exempt from the capital gains tax since 1969. Today it is estimated that the trust is worth in excess of $600 million.
It seems to me when we are asking single parents who earn less than $20,000 a year to pay taxes and when we are asking old age pensioners with incomes of less than $1,000 a month to pay taxes, we could ask wealthy families who hold assets in the area of $600 million to pay their fair share of taxes and not give them any further extensions or exemptions.
This exemption or extension costs the average Canadian money because we have to increase taxes on working families in order to make up for the loss of revenue. As a result of the fact that we do not have

details on family trusts the loss of revenue can only be estimated. A conservative estimate is that if only 1 per cent of the $70 billion in trust was subject to tax in a year at a marginal tax rate of 30 per cent it would raise over $200 million.
To make up $200 million we have to increase the taxes on working families or forgo vital programs in this country, programs that would create jobs or benefit people, such as day care. This $200 million would pay for half of the estimated cost of a universal day care program in Canada. We are all paying for this kind of tax policy.
This is not only the opinion of people in the New Democratic Party. There are also a number of tax professionals who share this view. Sidney Goldstein of Goldstein, Goldstein and Goldstein in Ottawa has said:
There is no question that it represents a massive windfall for existing trusts.
Kathryn Bush of Blake Cassels has said:
A cynical person might suggest that pressure from influential political supporters also should be listed as a reason for the draft legislation.
That is influential political supporters who have large assets. Neil Brooks, associate dean of Osgoode Hall Law School, has said:
The government has given Canada's wealthiest families notice that it intends to give them a gift worth several billion dollars.
I am pleased to be able to support this amendment but I find myself smiling a little because the 21-year rule was introduced by the Liberals. It is obvious from reading Hansard of February 23, 1993 that even in the last two months the Liberals have done a flip-flop.
At that point the member for Sudbury made it quite clear that the Liberals supported the government's extension of the family trust beyond the 21-year period and was quite critical of the fact that the NDP would oppose it.
Now the same member is the one who has made a motion to delete this section. I am sure it is like many other policies that the Liberals expound in that if they really sat down and looked at it they would understand that the NDP position is the correct position.

Mr. Speaker, it is truly amazing that we are sitting today in the House of Commons and we have a government that puts closure on a bill just a day after it was introduced. The closure it has put on the bill is very significant.
This bill amends the Income Tax Act. According to the experts, a couple of deans of law schools in Canada, from the University of Victoria and the associate dean of Osgoode Hall, tax experts who appeared before the committee, this piece of legislation will give the biggest tax break to billionaires and multimillionaires that some of them can think of in our entire history. This bill that is going through the House would give the biggest tax break to multimillionaires and billionaires.
The government stands today and puts closure on it. In other words, we have one day, today, for report stage and one more day on third reading. Why would the government do that? If any Canadians who are today filling out their income tax returns knew what we are doing in this Chamber they would be so shocked that if they could only organize themselves, 14.7 million ordinary Canadian taxpayers, they would march on this place.
It is going through too fast.

That is right. It is going through and nobody knows, but if they only knew what the Government of Canada was doing they would march on this place. This is the same Parliament which sat down just recently, and what did we do? We changed the Income Tax Act so that if the income tax department owes people money after April 30 the interest does not accumulate until 45 days after the date they file or April 30, whichever is later. However, if people owe the department money their interest comes due on April 30. This Parliament did that. This sitting of Parliament did that.
If people do not put their social insurance number down or supply it to somebody making out an information slip they are liable to a $100 fine these days. If they do not have one they have 15 days to apply and 15 days to produce it. As a result of a law passed by this Parliament if people file and have it postmarked May 1 they are given a penalty of 5 per cent on top of the taxes they owe, plus 1 per cent for every month after that up to 12 months.

This is the same Parliament that sat down and is today giving this incredible tax break to the wealthiest people in Canada. This is the same Parliament that approved a rule just recently affecting people who owe money to the Unemployment Insurance Commission. Every week now the unemployment insurance offices are sending a list of names over to the Department of National Revenue. Any rebates owed by the revenue department to those individuals who owe money to the Unemployment Insurance Commission beyond two years, if they are not drawing unemployment insurance and in the past year if they are drawing unemployment insurance, is deducted from what they have due to them from the tax department.
That would all be fine if the system that judges whether people owe money to the Unemployment Insurance Commission was fair, but it is not fair. The Parliament that is today giving this incredible tax break to billionaires in Canada is the same Parliament that changed the rules this year so that if people owed money or the student loans people claimed they owed money from 1960 or 1970, it is now automatically deducted from any rebates that they have coming back to them from the income tax department.
All those measures we have dealt with in this Chamber changed the Income Tax Act to really sock it to ordinary people, to add on as much interest as we can, to get to ordinary taxpayers and really slam it to them, without telling them what is available under the Income Tax Act, without suggesting to the students in Canada who are working, who went to work for the summer, that they can actually get moving expenses claimed on their income tax returns. There is no mention of that.
This year, on April 1, old age pensions, guaranteed income supplements and spousal allowances will be decided on the basis of last year's income. A lot of people are going to get a shock because of what we did in this Chamber, in that we approved a government measure to make payments to people; for example, in the fishing industry to buy back their salmon licences. We approved a measure for $8,000 to buy back people's licences, and now they are going to discover that it is going to be taken off the spousal allowance and the guaranteed income supplement this month. The government has done all those things to save money.
The government has introduced the GST. It has done whatever it could to cut back, to grab more money and to tax people more. The rich are getting richer; the poor are getting poorer; and the middle class is getting the shaft. Here it is today in this House passing a bill and putting closure on it. In other words it is saying we are not allowed to debate it any more today or tomorrow.
This is a bill that according to the experts in Canada is a big giveaway. It is not according to the politicians and we have to make that distinction. The standing committee had its meetings and they were a total embarrassment. The Standing Committee on Finance of this House of Commons had hearings that were to most Canadians a total embarrassment. The headlines in The Gazette of Montreal said: "Officials rush to committee meeting because experts say big giveaway to billionaires". That was on the business page last Friday. The story explained that some of the experts in Canada appearing before the committee said that this is the biggest giveaway to the biggest corporations, all those multimultimillionaires and 20 or so billionaires.
It is mentioned many times in many documents that we are very fortunate in Canada to have one of the highest numbers of billionaires per capita in the industrialized nations and we have a system in which it is possible to make a lot of money. These witnesses were saying that this is the biggest giveaway to them.
Then we had the revenue department and the finance department rush into the committee to try to contradict what was being said. That is what was in the newspapers. That is what is true. Do we know what they said to the committee? The finance officials of this government and Revenue Canada had to turn around and say that they did not know how much money was involved in this bill. They do not even know.
Members of Parliament standing on the government side do not know how much money is involved in this bill. All we can do is take the word of the experts that this is the biggest tax giveaway probably in our history, putting off the paying of taxes for another 30 years for a select group of people in our society.
This bill is putting off the payment while we bring people into the Tax Court of Canada, sock it to them and then we try to develop a defence for some of these

people while this is going on in the Elouse of Commons. This is a total embarrassment. I would like government members to stand and explain why they are changing the law.

Mr. Speaker, the changes in Bill C-92 to the 21-year rule for trusts are intended to ensure that the original purpose for the rule is in fact achieved. The purpose is to ensure that the wealth accumulated during an individual's lifetime cannot be transferred from one generation to another without first being taxed.
With your permission, Mr. Speaker, let us talk a little bit about the purpose of the 21-year rule. The 21-year rule was introduced in 1972 as part of the capital gains regime. It is a necessary part of the income tax rules which tax accrued gains on death, intended to ensure that wealth accumulated during an individual's lifetime cannot be transferred from one generation to another without first being taxed.
As the Minister of Finance indicated at the time the rule was introduced, the 21-year rule was necessary to prevent the indefinite postponement of capital gains tax through the use of long-term trusts. The postponement of such tax would otherwise be possible using trusts under which individual beneficiaries have the right to trust income during their lifetimes but no interest in trust capital. No gains on death would arise in respect of such life interests since they have no value after the holder dies.
Why are changes needed? On February 11, 1991 draft legislation was released proposing changes to the 21-year rule. These changes, together with minor revisions resulting from subsequent consultations, are contained in Bill C-92. They address two serious problems with the existing legislation while ensuring that the original purpose underlying the rule is met and the related tax revenues are secured.
First, for many trusts it is possible to defeat the intent of the 21-year rule by transferring property from one trust to a newly created trust with a new 21-year period. Second, the existing 21-year rule penalizes those trusts which cannot because of their particular terms distribute their assets before 1993. This is particularly the case with trusts which were settled before the rule was introduced.
Government Orders
I would like to say a few words on what are the changes. The proposed changes will ensure that the 21-year period cannot be refreshed by transferring trust assets to new trusts. They will also allow a trust which has been settled for an individual's children to elect to defer the deemed disposition that would otherwise occur under the 21-year rule until the death of the last such child.
Where a trust elects under the new rules gains which have accrued on assets it holds at that time, as well as gains which subsequently accrue on all trust assets, it will become taxable on the death of the last beneficiary who is not more than one generation removed from the trust settlor, or on the earlier sale of such assets. A trust that elects will not thereafter be permitted to distribute trust assets on a rollover basis, as described, to beneficiaries who are more than one generation removed from the trust settlor.
With this election the capital gains tax consequences will be the same whether an individual makes a gift of property directly to his or her child or makes the gift to a trust for the benefits of such child. In either case there will be a recognition for tax purposes on any accrued gains on the property at the time of the gift, and there will be a recognition of future gains with respect to the growth in value of the property gifted no later than the death of the child. This is consistent with the principle that wealth accumulation should be taxed in the hands of each generation.
I will say a few words on how the rule operates. The 21-year rule requires that the value of trust assets be determined every 21 years, beginning in 1993. Any accrued capital gains in excess of accrued capital losses on assets which are in a trust at that time are subject to income tax in the year in the same way as realized capital gains and losses. As a result the 21-year rule subjects to capital gains tax only those gains which have accrued after 1971.
It is important to note that the 21-year rule was not intended to prevent the distribution of trust assets to the beneficiaries of the trust before the 21-year period expires. Such distributions are consistent with the objective of the rule itself. Specific income tax rules provide for a rollover of trust property to the beneficiaries in accordance with the terms of the trust. These rollover

rules recognize that because trust assets are simply being held for trust beneficiaries, their subsequent distribution to beneficiaries should not be a taxable event.
Later, when a beneficiary dies or actually sells the assets, any gains which have accumulated while the assets were held in the trust, as well as in the beneficiary's hands, are taxable at that time.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased I am back today to speak on this clause of the bill.
It is one that has caused most Canadians who understand what is going on in this omnibus legislation dealing with taxation a great deal of concern. As usual, when the government is trying to do some favours for its friends, who normally are not the poor or the destitute or those who have to rely on food banks to feed their children because of this government's policy, it tries to hide it. That is exactly what the government has done in this legislation.
It came in with a paper about two years ago and in the paper was a press release. It was pretty innocuous and hardly anybody picked it up at the time. The government said in the release that basically by regulation and now by law it was going to exempt some of Canada's wealthiest families from paying taxes on assets that have been in trust for 21 years. What does that mean to the average Canadian?
Most people did not understand. Most people were worried at that point, as I said, about trying to feed their kids. They were worrying about whether or not they were going to have a job next week because of the recession. During that period the government tried to sneak in a regulation, a change in the law which was not going to put them back to work, which was not going to shorten the lines at the food banks, which was not going to address the whole range of structural problems in the economy caused by Tory economics. They were simply interested in helping their friends, not just the friends who have a few thousands of dollars, not the friends who have a few hundreds of thousands of dollars-they had already looked after them-not their friends that had a few million dollars, but their friends in some cases who have billions of dollars in assets which are shielded effectively from taxation by regulation in the tax law.
.(1135)
It is a regulation that expired. The provision expired. The 21-year rule expired. The growth in value of the assets that were in family trusts were supposed to be taxable. As my friend from Gander just said, that was not good enough for the government. It has done this at a time when it is going around cutting and slashing every program of which it can possibly think.
Let us look at what the government has done in the last few years. It says there is no money out there. It has had over 40 tax increases, most of them affecting disproportionately the middle classes. There have been over 40 tax increases since this bunch opposite came into power. The average Canadian family in constant dollars is paying more than $2,000 in additional taxes because of all the changes this bunch opposite has made.
The government has assaulted the middle income, lower middle income and low income groups. The middle income group to which most Canadians watching this belong, the working class that tries to keep one step ahead of the sheriff, that tries to keep the kids clothed and fed in a modest home somewhere, the people who work hard for a modest living, count for about 37 per cent of the wealth in Canada. Under this bunch opposite, the government has increased the tax burden on this particular group, the average Canadian, so that the group which has control of 37 per cent of the wealth in the country pays 52 per cent of the taxes.
The government says that everybody has to suffer because there is no money out there. This is the same group which has told us it will no longer be participating 50 cents on every dollar for health care.
What does that mean? It means the impact of four successive Tory budgets on my province of Nova Scotia has been tremendous. The federal government has withdrawn, just this year past, health care expenditures of $111 million from a province of 885,000 people.
It has cut back on its cost sharing on post-secondary education in the province of Nova Scotia by $47 million. It says it does not have money. It has increased taxes. It has hiked them. It has decreased its level of participation in programs because it does not have the money and generally it has been going around telling everybody that

March 30, 1993

we have to do more with less but we have to give them more to do it with.
When it comes to the wealthiest of Canadians, individuals that have established family trusts, they are given another tax holiday. The government is giving a tax holiday on billions and billions of dollars that are in family trusts. As my colleague said, there are up to 30 years of additional tax holidays. I was outraged when this issue first came up, as were people in my constituency.
There was an article by Neil Brooks about a year and a half ago. One of the problems we have is that the government, which has information about the value of these trusts that would allow us as members of Parliament to figure out how much taxes would be owed if it had allowed the 21-year rule to expire and had not tried to replace it with this new law, does not want to tell us the information. In this article by Neil Brooks it is indicated that one of the items that was removed in 1972 was the federal inheritance tax. That action resulted in a lump sum gift of about $12.5 billion to Canada's richest families. That is according to a calculation by John Bossons, University of Toronto economist. That was back in 1972.
These trusts are now probably worth $50 billion, maybe more. The government says: "Sorry, if you are on social assistance in British Columbia, Alberta or Ontario which used to be have provinces but not any more that is too bad".
The federal government has frozen its rate of participation on social assistance. It has capped CAP. So if you are out there, sorry. The poor are going to have to do with less. If you need health care in Nova Scotia you may not be able to find a hospital bed because these guys have cut back. If you are a university student in Newfoundland your tuition will be higher because the federal government has cut back by about $32 million on its cost sharing of post-secondary educational institutions in that province.
However, if you are one of Canada's richest Canadians you are going to have another 30-year tax holiday. Just keep rolling that money around within the trust, taking all the benefits from it and we are going to keep away from it. At this very time that the government talks

about the need for restraint and the need to increase revenues it is allowing billions of dollars, not thousands, not millions, in tax revenue to be legally avoided by Canada's richest families. This is an affront.
It is an affront to the senior citizen who might be living on an income of $18,000 a year. I had somebody say to me the other day: "I am mad as hell. I make $18,000 per year. I put some money away. I get a little annuity. And the government tells me that I have to pay the government quarterly instalments on income tax. When I tell them I do not have the money to pay at the end of the year they charge me interest on the quarterly instalments that I did not make. Mr. MacDonald, I do not have enough money to live. What in the name of goodness, this government does not just want my money at the end of the year. It is taxing me all through the year for the money as it comes in. I have worked hard to build this country. I have put a little money aside; I salted some money away. Why are they coming after me?"
That is a good question. About six months ago a lady came to see me. Her husband had died. She had never been in the work force. She had a small pension. She never had to look after the bills, never had to do the books. She did not file her deceased husband's Revenue Canada forms on time. When she did she was billed $750 for the fine and interest. She did not know what to do with it. She was making $972 a month to live on, to pay for her mortgage, food, heat and lights. However, an order was put against her pension. The government took $200 a month from her $900-plus pension. Is that the type of fairness this government thinks Canadians want in their tax system?
I think Canadians are outraged that the government has this particular clause in this legislation. I hope the government is taken to the cleaners when it goes to the electorate for this type of activity, this type of legislated unfairness which is for those who have at the expense of those who have not. We will not be supporting this bill because of it.

Mr. Speaker, I listened attentively to my hon. friend from Dartmouth and he accused the government of doing things. He says the government is doing things for its friends with this bill. That is what he said.

The friends of the government are the same friends of the Liberal Party. Who initiated this trust fund in 1972? The Pierre Elliott Trudeau government of 1972. The Eatons, the Molsons, the Bronfmans, the Seagrams and the Irvings from down east all put the pressure on the Liberals when they were the government. Now suddenly they are going to vote against the bill. They are going to vote against the Frankenstein which they created. Mary Shelley would be appalled. At least you do not destroy your own creation. This was their own creation in 1972.
What do we have? Twenty-one years. For 21 years the wealthiest families in this country were able to put aside in trust accounts what we now estimate to be somewhere in the vicinity of $70 billion.
We hear it every day from across the way: "We are in tough times. We have to put our economic house in order. We have to watch our credit rating. We are living beyond our means. We have to cut back services. The people have to pay more because we have to reduce this deficit''.
The member for Halton-Peel who is running now for the Tory leadership even had the little newspaper delivery boys put in their $2.40 a week toward debt reduction. Is that not the most ridiculous thing? There is a clock showing the debt and deficit reduction and this little boy has finished his paper route and is bringing his offerings up to the altar of the privileged. He is offering his $2.40 to reduce the deficit.
Then we have people who have money. Why is the government always taxing people who do not have money? There is a trust fund with approximately $70 billion in it and we cannot get one plug nickel out of it to help pay the costs of running this country and to help reduce the deficit. That is a phoney argument.
Let us draw a contrast with how the government treats another trust fund. With respect to family trusts, it will exempt them for another 21 years, probably another 38 years. How does it treat another trust fund? I will talk about another trust fund.
It is called the funeral trusts. Older Canadians in particular in making arrangements to pay for their burial put money into a funeral trust fund. It is usually run by
the funeral parlour. What is this government proposing to do? It is proposing to reach right into the funeral trusts and tax the interest accrued on the funds in the funeral trust fund. It is financial necrophilia. That is what it is.
It is what?

Financial necrophilia. I know there is the common saying that you cannot take it with you, but this government every day is proving that it is going to take it off you before you go into the next world.
Here we have the prospect of one family trust with a considerable amount of money in it, $70 billion. Approximately $400 million is in the accumulated funeral trust in the province of Ontario. The government is going to reach into this trust fund and tax the interest accruing on the funeral trusts. This is money set aside by individuals so that they will not be a burden on their families when they die. Their funerals will be paid for. The interest that accrues in that fund is to offset inflation and to pay for their burial costs. Mr. Speaker, I too want to say a few words about the bill before the House today regarding tax changes in our country and in particular the question of family trusts in Bill C-92.
As my friend from Nickel Belt has said, the whole question of family trusts began back in 1972 when we dealt with estate taxes and capital gains taxes in this House. The Liberal Party was in power with then Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau.
There was a tremendous lobby at that time from some of the wealthiest families in this country to set up a tax loophole for them and for their families. It was to give them 21 years of protection during which they did not have to pay taxes.
Over the years billions and billions of dollars have been put into these family trusts. We have privacy laws in this country so we are not sure how much money has accumulated. Of course we need those privacy laws. The estimate we have from people in the field is that around $70 billion has now been accumulated in family trusts by higher income families and is tax exempt under present law for 21 years. After 21 years arrangements were to be made where taxes would be paid in the appropriate manner on the money by some of the wealthiest families in this country.
The 21 years are up. It is now 1993 and what has happened? Lobbyists have gone to the government across the way and said: "These poor families in this country are going to have to pay some taxes. We need an

extension of the 21 years". The government has now tabled Bill C-92 before the House to extend that 21-year period until the last exempt beneficiary of that trust passes away.
What does that mean? It means now that instead of 21 years those trusts may run for 30, 40, 75 or even 80 years or more if a young child has been made part of that trust. It is not fair, just or proper that the wealthiest families shall now be paying hundreds of millions of dollars less in taxes than they would be if we kept the law in place with the 21-year limitation. Perhaps medicare would be better protected for the ordinary

people or the family allowance program would not have had to be abolished. The old age pensions could be adjusted to give our senior citizens a better income to live their last few years in our land.
There are many ways we could use the money from the trust funds. We now have a debt of about $450 billion. It was about $200 billion when the Conservatives took office some eight or nine years ago. I suggest if one looks at the income tax returns year after year one finds that many of these wealthy Canadians and big corporations are very generous contributors to the Conservative Party of Canada in terms of their electoral funds and funds for the ongoing operations of the Conservative Party. These people are now saying that 21 years is over when they have been exempt from taxes and they want it extended. They lobby the government. It is an election year and of course the government brings in Bill C-92, part of which is to extend the 21-year limit of tax exempt status to family trusts. If this bill passes which it will because of the Conservative majority, it will abolish the 21-year limitation and allow these family trusts to sit on tax until the last exempt beneficiary dies. In many of these cases that will be 30, 40, 50, 80 or even 90 years.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to add a few comments to this debate because a lot of comment from the other side of the House has distorted some of the elements of the question of trusts and what they do.
Government Orders
I am not here to speak in support of trusts or say who should or should not be taxed. However, I think we should try to put this in perspective and understand what we are dealing with. We should not allow too much misinformation so people think trusts are something they are not.
It is important to recognize that trusts are created for a variety of reasons and in some cases have tax consequences. Putting assets in a trust does not mean that all of a sudden no tax is paid. Income from those trusts is taxed every year just like other taxpayers. If there is income from regular sources or capital gains trusts are treated the same as any other taxpayer and, for that matter, are taxed at the top rate of income tax every year.
They do not necessarily get the benefits of an individual taxpayer who would have other benefits which would reduce that top rate of income tax. We are talking about assets that have been put into a trust for one reason or another and when they should be taxed just simply because they have been accumulating wealth for an individual during his lifetime.
Prior to 1972 there was an estate tax. When people died they were taxed based on the value of their estates or the assets they had at that time. In 1972 a capital gains tax system was implemented. That means when people sell or dispose of assets those gains are taxed. They are taxed when the person transfers those assets to the trust. It could be said that the person has chosen to have died earlier because by transferring those assets to the trust those assets are then subject to tax at that time. Otherwise those assets would have remained not subject to tax and not taxed until the death of the taxpayer.
Setting up a trust advances the time of the tax and the tax applies when the trust is set up. The change in this rule allows those trusts to continue to be reinvigorated and transferred from one trust to another without tax being paid. In some cases it prevents this.
In the case of beneficiaries this change deems that where the assets are in a trust they will not be taxable or can be chosen not to be taxable until the last beneficiary of the person who set up the trust dies. In other words the treatment becomes the same as if the person distributed his or her assets directly to the beneficiary.

March 30, 1993
Government Orders
We are not saying tax is never paid. First, tax is paid when the trust is set up as if the taxpayer setting up the trust had disposed of those assets at that time. Second, trusts are taxed on an annual basis just like any other taxpayer. Finally we are saying they will be taxed when they are either distributed to the beneficiary or the last beneficiary of the trust dies.
It has been suggested that billions of dollars are involved here. That is simply not true. Most of the trusts affected by this rule in the absence of these changes would simply distribute their assets in any event. Income taxes will be paid by the beneficiaries when the assets are sold or when the beneficiary dies. In such cases the new rules do not change either the amount or the timing of the tax paid.
We could revert to a system of inheritance tax on death and eliminate the capital gains tax where in many cases we tax people in advance of dying. That was the objective of the Benson tax reform at that time. As has been pointed out, the Liberal government of the day did not want to allow capital gains to build up for years and years. It decided to tax them on an interim basis such as when people sold them. If they did not sell them they would become taxable on death, or in the case of transferring them to a trust they would become taxable at that time. We chose to collect taxes sooner than the pre-1972 system. That is the result of some of these changes. What we do not do or seek to do, however, is tax them twice, tax them both on the distribution to the beneficiary and on an annual basis or every time the gain is realized. We could choose to do that. We could double tax them but I do not think anybody here is suggesting we do that.
What is being suggested is that somehow these trusts avoid taxes and no one ever pays any tax on them. That is simply not true. What it does in most cases is it advances certain taxes that are paid to a time prior to when they would otherwise be paid.
We should try to determine whether these rules are appropriate or whether we should change to some other form such as an inheritance tax. If that is what is being suggested by the opposition parties then I think it is a fair suggestion. In my view it is probably a good idea and one we should examine.
I do not think we should allow the misunderstanding to be perpetuated, that somehow trusts simply are vehicles
by which wealthy people avoid tax and never pay any tax. They are part of the over-all tax regime. In a number of cases, including the changes in these rules, trusts are forced to pay taxes every 21 years rather than only when the person setting up the trust dies. In other words, in many cases with the 21-year rule trusts will be taxed every 21 years. We will be taxing those benefits or those accrued gains sooner rather than later. When later comes there will be less tax payable because they will have been taxed on an ongoing basis.

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to engage in this debate, not so much as a matter of the rhetoric of tax reform and the partisan differences but to try to get a few concepts clear.
Perhaps because of my background I find it very offensive when some speakers, such as the last speaker from the NDP, the second to last speaker in the House, stands and flagrantly misrepresents the nature of the taxation regime that exists and the changes that were introduced in the reform of 1971-72.
I understand that some of these issues are complex and difficult but a few points should be made. First, and the speaker who spoke previously mentioned this, trusts are a fundamental part of our system of law, not just tax law but private law.
When I practised law most of the wills I prepared for people with children contained trust provisions, not because they were rich, not because they were some kind of an elite wealthy group, but because they did not want their children to inherit, usually life insurance proceeds, before they were old enough to manage the money. So a trust was set up in the will. Veiy often it required that the child reach age 25, sometimes older, before he or she received the capital assets of the trust. They could be quite considerable, even for somebody of modest means who invested heavily in life insurance in the event of their death.
These trusts exist in many cases. They are carrying on, they are continuous, and they are taxed just as all trusts are taxed. When the NDP member from Saskatchewan gets up and says that the Liberals brought in a law whereby trusts were not taxed for 21 years, he is simply not stating what is true. It is not correct.
I am sure it is difficult for people to understand the difference between taxing income and taxing capital. But if we do not have some understanding of what that
March 30, 1993

means, we cannot understand what the provision is that we are debating here.
Income is the amount that we earn on a continuing basis. If a person has a Canada Savings Bond, the bond itself represents capital and the interest received on it is income. The income of trusts is and always has been taxed. It was taxed prior to 1972. It is taxed subsequent to 1972. If the trust is set up between people who were alive that income is not taxed the same way an individual's income is taxed. It is taxed at a higher rate. It is taxed from the first dollar at the maximum rate of tax for individuals.
If the trust is one such as I referred to in my example in a will, the income is taxed every year just as an individual's income is taxed. The difference is the trust does not get the personal and dependent exemptions that an individual has to rely on. Either way, income earned on an annual basis is and has been taxed.
What about capital gains? What is a capital gain? Perhaps a person owns a piece of land, a small apartment building, a duplex or shares in a corporation that can be sold on the stock exchange. Any time one of these is disposed of and there is a profit over and above what was paid for the asset, there is a capital gain. It is taxed as income in Canada, subject to the fact that we reduce the total gain to 75 per cent for the purposes of determining taxable income. The lower rate reflects the fact that we do not take inflation into account. If a property was bought in 1971 and sold this year, 22 years later, there is a gain on it. We do not take into account inflation. We only require the person to include 75 per cent of the gain in income.
There are debates about whether it is fair, whether it is the right number, whether it should apply to all gains or whether it should be long-term gains as opposed to short-term gains. I will not get into that today. The principle is this, gains are taxed.
When my friend from the NDP says that the Liberals introduced a loophole in 1971, what he is failing to mention is that prior to 1972 capital gains were not taxed at all. Zero per cent of the gain was included in income, not just for trusts but for individuals and corporations as
Government Orders
well. Capital gains were not taxed. In 1971 under the tax reform of that year, for the first time capital gains were included in income for taxation purposes. This was a major reform, arguably the most important reform in our income tax law since income tax was introduced in 1917.
What do we do with trusts? It is very easy with individuals. We determine the capital gain either when they dispose of the property, when they give it away to somebody or when they die. That is easy, no problem. What do we do with trusts? A trust is a legal concept which has permanence in our British system of law. It has some correlations in the French civil code but it is not exactly the same. It is an ancient concept. Trusts do not die. Trusts do not die, so how do we determine their capital gains?
If the property is sold that is when they realize a capital gain. It is taxed. There is no difference there between a trust and an individual. The problem is this. Some trusts, depending on their terms, can literally go on forever. What is the answer? The answer that was proposed in 1971 is to say 21 years is a long enough trust and every 21 years whether the property is disposed of or not it will be deemed to have been sold even if it has not and capital gains tax will have to be paid.
It did not seem unduly harsh at the time and I have to say it does not seem unduly harsh to me today. That is why I oppose the amendment that the government is proposing. People need to understand what the concept was that this rule was trying to get at. NDP members like to say it is a big loophole. The fact that there is a 21-year delay they allege is a loophole.
I asked the member from Saskatchewan earlier what he would do. He did not have an answer. Are they proposing that all capital gains realized or unrealized in trusts be taxed on an annual basis? Is that what they are proposing? If so, why do they not say so? Why do they not say that they want all those little trusts out there- many of them are not very big-which are established for the benefit of children, to hire appraisers every year, to hire expensive accountants every year to figure out a complicated tax return every year for these trusts that are really only going to be set up for five to ten years?

March 30, 1993
Government Orders
Why do they not admit that is what they want to do? Why do they not admit that they want to bring a system of market value assessment on an annual basis into our income tax law so that every year we are having to appraise all of our assets? That is the kind of intermeddling stupidity that the NDP has become famous for in the province of Ontario. They are not honest enough to admit that is what they want to do.
The proposal put forward in 1971 made sense. It gave the trusts a lot of time to make their arrangements. To plan 21 years is a long time in anyone's lifetime. I do not understand why the government feels that at the last minute it has to say it is going to grant a reprieve. I simply do not understand.
I do not agree the numbers that have been spouted by some members on how much is out there are valid. I do not think there is any way of knowing how much tax might be generated with the 21-year realization. I think it is fair to say it is a considerable amount of money.
With the current fiscal situation the government is in and the reasonableness of the test passed in 1972,1 fail to see why this amendment has been brought forward by the government.

I fail to recognize why this government would choose to single out the owners of small apartment buildings and deny them something that they are allowing other members of the Canadian community, namely to realize a capital gains of $100,000 tax-free.
I often wondered whether the government was doing this on purpose. Was it really aware it was doing this? It was very much aware that all these ordinary Canadians would now be fully taxed on any gains on their small apartment building. It just did not make sense to me. That is one of the reasons I oppose this particular measure. If the government wishes to say that there will be no more capital

gains exemptions because it can no longer afford this gift to people, that is fine.
If that is what it would like to do then do it. These same property owners have been dealt some very serious blows in our economy. Rent controls have caused them extremely serious problems. Most people now would not buy an investment property because it just is not worth while.

I can afford to give you a tax break" or "I cannot afford to give you a tax break". I say to this government that it should make up its mind which way it wants it. Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words in support of my hon. friend, the hon. member for Sudbury, and the amendment put forward by her.
The member put it quite well. On one hand the government says it is going to give a capital gains break to somebody who buys a race horse in Kentucky, Texas, or in any of the other states in the United States where they are in the business of breeding race horses. They buy the race horse. If there is a gain realized from the race horse, the government says: "That is fine. We will give you a tax break". On the other hand, there is a

March 30, 1993
Government Orders
different type of capital gain, namely something that pertains to property in Canada, on which it will not allow that same exemption.
A moment ago members of the NDP were making reference to me, saying that I was embarrassed about this entire question of capital gains that was brought in by the Liberals. I want to thank the hon. member for Ottawa South for explaining what happened in 1972.
As we know, Canada did away with the inheritance tax, the estate tax as it was called at the time, in 1971. We had an inheritance tax just like they do in the United States today.
If one dies in the United States today and one has any amount of property, by law it all has to be assessed. If it is found that the market value of the property is worth more than $600,000, it is taxed. I do not know what the rate is now. It used to be 55 per cent of the value of property that was judged to be in excess of $600,000. It is called the inheritance tax.
We had such a tax in Canada prior to 1972. The tax kicked in at somewhere around $150,000. If the value of all property was judged to be in excess of that, it kicked in at a rate of 15 per cent or 10 cent and went up progressively from there.
That was the situation prior to 1972. The law was changed in 1971, taking effect in 1972, to replace the inheritance tax.
Canada does not have an inheritance tax any more. It was replaced by the capital gains tax, which in 1972 when it was brought in was 50 per cent of the normal rate of taxation.
When the Canadian government brought in that law instituting the capital gains tax and doing away with the inheritance tax, it did not create loopholes; it tried to plug the loopholes. The 21-year rule was in my humble opinion an effort to plug a loophole. As the previous speaker from Ottawa South pointed out, a trust does not die. An individual dies but a trust just does not die.
The problem was what to do when somebody had their assets in a trust and the deemed value of those assets would normally become taxable upon death. What if it is
put into a trust prior to that moment in time and of course the trust cannot die?
One must lay down a law so that at the end of every 21 years all the assets in that trust and the accrued value of the capital gains on the assets would come due. One would say that the trust would have been deemed to have died at that moment in time at 21 years.
That was not a loophole created by the Liberals. That was a plugging of a loophole by the Liberals that would have seen, according to the testimony before the committee, vast sums of money now coming into the public Treasury because of that capital gains provision in 1993.
This would have been very handy for the Government of Canada at this moment in time when it is trying to get money here and trying to get money there. That is why quite frankly we are puzzled as to why the Government of Canada would forgo that kind of revenue at this moment in time.
I wish to raise on this particular amendment proposed by my hon. friend a serious problem relating to capital gains and the capital gains exemption. The Government of Canada has throughout the past two years given certain payments to individuals in Canada that have been judged to be capital gains and that qualify for the capital gains exemption under the $100,000 exemption.
A lot of these payments have been given in our agricultural industry, farming industry and fishing industry. They are the primary industries. The payments have been for people to get out of the business they are doing.
In other words the Government of Canada has come along and said: "Look, we are going to give you a payment". In my particular case on my coastline of Newfoundland it says: "We are going to give you money for selling your licences back to us so we can get you out of the fishery". In this case it was in particular salmon licences. However, it says that it qualifies for the capital gains exemption that we are talking about today because it says it is property. That is what it was judged to be.
However, in offering the money to Canadians and saying to Canadians: "Look, we will judge this to be a capital gain to qualify under the capital gains exemption", they forgot to tell those Canadians 60 years of age or older that the Department of National Health and Welfare has a rule. It says that if one receives money in
March 30, 1993

the previous year as a capital gain that has to be subtracted from the guaranteed income supplement and the spousal allowance in the following year.
This means that right now under the capital gains and the capital gains exemption which was granted last year, hundreds and hundreds and hundreds of people over 60 years of age are receiving notification this week and next week that their spousal allowance has now been cancelled because of the capital gain and the capital gains exemption last year and that the guaranteed income supplement has been reduced accordingly.
I raise the point in discussion today about this capital gains exemption and the subject of the capital gains and the capital gains exemption as it relates to this particular bill. Hopefully somebody in the ministry will see the light and pass a minute of cabinet that says persons who received this money and who had an income that normally gave them the spousal allowance and the guaranteed income supplement would be exempt as far as capital gains and the capital gains exemption of last year is concerned in their guaranteed income supplement and in their spousal allowance, both of which are about to change in April.
I will get back for the minute that I have left to the proposal put forward by the representative of the Liberal Party. Why would one bring in a change in one's capital gains exemption that would say that one is not going to encourage people to build buildings, homes or apartment buildings, but one is going to encourage people to buy race horses in Kentucky? That is the essence of the amendment we are talking about today.
On that basis I would have to strongly support the proposal put forward by my hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment, just to put it in context, proposed by the Liberal member for Sudbury would retain the $100,000 capital gains exemption for people who invest in real estate.
In a way this amendment gives me some problem because I personally feel that the $100,000 capital gains exemption should be abolished altogether. I support the capital gains exemption for farmers and for small busi-
Govemment Orders
ness people who dispose of the shares of their small business because this is one of the key ways in which people in those categories are able to provide for then-own retirement.
With respect to the $100,000 capital gains exemption this has been in operation since 1985 at a lower rate and then was gradually built up to where it is now. I think the minister of the day proposed to bring it up to $500,000, but it was finally stopped at $100,000. The evidence is that this benefit accrues only to those who are in a high income category and therefore have lots of cash available to put into investments. I do not think the government has been able to produce any evidence whatsoever that it has stimulated investment or, in other words, that it has caused people who would otherwise have consumed their savings to have instead directed it into an investment which would go to create jobs in Canada.
In the absence of that evidence I do not understand really the rationale for having the $100,000 capital gains exemption at all. However, if we are going to have it, is it not peculiar that the government has decided to exempt investment real estate from it?
Let us make another thing clear. This proposal from the Liberal member for Sudbury does not suggest including real estate in the exemption that is not investment related. In other words, this is not a way of reopening it for second family homes to get into the exempt category. It is a proposal for people who want to invest in a duplex, a triplex, a little apartment building or a little commercial property, to give them the same benefit as the government is permitting to continue to accrue to those who go to their local broker and buy shares in a company.
With respect, I do not understand that rationale. Very often it is the small real estate investor, often a firsttime home buyer who buys a duplex and rents out the other half, a small business person or a comer store operator who rents out an adjacent apartment or has some investment in real estate involved in their assets. They are not usually incorporated. They are usually small, low end and unincorporated.
The NDP in Ontario has done everything it can to destroy the real estate investment market in the province of Ontario. If one wants to find commercial real

March 30, 1993
Government Orders
estate for a bargain price, I suggest Ontario and especially Toronto.
What the NDP has done cannot be offset by permitting a $100,000 capital gains exemption for investors in real estate because frankly there are no capital gains in real estate at the present time in Ontario any way. Perhaps times will change and things will improve.
However, to put it in the most cynical way possible, it seems to me that the government in bringing in this amendment is favouring the brokerage industry by permitting people to get the capital gains exemption if they invest through a broker in listed stock but not if they buy a small piece of real estate and try to make a little bit of a gain on it by renting it out and hoping that it increases in value over time.
If I had my way I would get rid of the exemption altogether, but if we are going to keep it for some kind of investment why target it for the blue chip stock and not for the little investment in a real estate property that so many small investors look to for the way of building a little bit of savings for their future?

Mr. Speaker, I too would like to speak on the proposed amendment of my colleague in our party from Sudbury with respect to the capital gains exemption.
I would like to touch on two areas that I think my colleague from Ottawa South pointed out. It was the philosophical issue as to whether or not one needs capital gains exemptions at all. However, I think one ought to look at the fairness of the tax system and the removal of this capital gains exemption as proposed by the government in this Bill C-92. Of course the Liberal amendment is to change that and to allow those exemptions to occur.
I guess I want to deal with two aspects. One aspect is with regard to the fairness of the government's move to eliminate the capital gains exemption from real estate. I think my colleague from Ottawa South touched on the reason why the government would only want to look at real estate and not at other opportunities where the capital gains exemption would remain.
I am in favour of the capital gains exemption at all levels. I believe there is a purpose to those capital gains exemption, that is to allow citizens no matter what
income stream they are in to invest in various opportunities such as business, stocks, real estate, farming or a number of other areas. I think that is an important policy matter for any government, but I believe we ought to encourage people to invest in their country in an indirect way by investing in business, real estate, farming or in other ways.
The incentive of capital gains exemption to the tune of $100,000 allows people to directly invest in their future and the country's future in opportunities not only for themselves but for their families and again their communities and their country. Therefore I think philosophically we ought to look at why one should have a capital gains exemption at all. I believe that those capital gains exemptions are there for a purpose, that is to stimulate investment, savings, activity, growth and job creation. One could make a very good case for those capital gains exemptions.
Therefore I believe it is punitive and unfair for the government to essentially say that capital gains exemptions are all right except for real estate. It is looking at one class of business and saying it will no longer be considered for the capital gains exemption. That should be taken into consideration. Our amendment tries to put everybody on the same footing in the same class.
Unlike the member for Ottawa South who might say for instance that we should get rid of all capital gains exemption, I come at it the other way and say that I believe in capital gains exemptions as an opportunity for job creation as well as wealth creation. That is fair. We approach the situation differently.
With respect to the specific benefits of this capital gains exemption, as the housing critic for my party I think it is fair to say that looking at the profile of the average person who invests in a duplex or triplex or a small apartment building the country and communities achieve a social benefit by those people investing in those kinds of properties.
We get a supply of housing stock which becomes affordable housing. If it is only left to the big guys, the big developers and contractors, the ones with the land to develop the apartments and so on, and not allow anybody else into the real estate market, I suggest we will not get affordable housing but the market will essentially be driven by very few people.
March 30, 1993

Government Orders
Members of the middle income group for a great many years have primarily been investing in these duplexes and triplexes. They want to provide for their own pensions, their own futures and those of their children, and do so by investing in real estate. They have also provided this country with a great supply of affordable housing. I believe the Canadian Real Estate Association and others have indicated that if this opportunity for people to invest in real estate is taken away, this country and its communities will be worse off in terms of affordable housing.
Before we go about trashing this capital gains exemption just because we want to get to the speculator, the person who in better times in an overheated inflationary market was able to take advantage of buying and selling, we can put in place certain safeguards to make sure that kind of speculation does not occur. But let us not take away a fantastic financial incentive mechanism for the average person to be able to invest in real estate.
Just like they will continue to be able to invest in stocks or businesses, let them continue to invest in real estate. The side benefit to the country and the community will be the great supply of affordable housing. We know how tragic it is that a lot of people are finding it very difficult to afford shelter. In fact, over 1.5 million people are putting over 30 per cent of their income toward housing. There are 500,000 people who are paying at least 50 per cent of their income toward housing.
There is an opportunity in having the average individual invest in rental income, be it another house, duplex or triplex. At the end of the day this country benefits by that investment. Yes, they do benefit themselves because of the tax write-offs and tax advantages, but they are also investing in their future, the creation of wealth and the future of their children.
I suggest this particular capital gains exemption which this government now wants to take away will be negative for the economy. It will not do anything in terms of creation of jobs or the creation of wealth in this country.
I support the amendment put forward by my colleague, the Liberal member for Sudbury. We should try to convince this government that if it wants to take away the speculative aspects of this particular exemption because it feels it may have been abused in the past, there are other ways of doing that other than trying to take away this exemption totally.
Again on the fairness aspect, why pick on the real estate or property end when in fact stocks, bonds and business investments are allowed to remain intact?
I believe in the whole concept of capital gains exemption. It is a great opportunity for people to invest for themselves, for their future, for their children's future and for this country in providing the prosperity and jobs the country needs.

Mr. Speaker, the particular provision in the statute has caused me considerable problems, but I think on balance there is some good rationale for the provision and the amendment ought to be defeated.
It is fair to say that of the capital gains claimed tax-free by the $100,000 exemption, over half of the gains for filing purposes have been claimed on small amounts of real estate. By and large, those items of real estate have been vacant land and property which is non-income producing.
The whole purpose of the exemption or allowance of $100,000 for capital gains was to direct investment into something that would spin the economy along. Investing in a vacant lot or investing in a cottage site, or just having an extra family home is not something that spins the economy along. The real question is: Should that kind of investment somehow be tax-free to the extent of $100,000?
It is the government's view if we are going to have allowances that reduce people's taxable income made by capital gains provisions it at least ought to be income derived from investment that is of a go-go nature. Therefore if one buys and invests in a mine or a business or buys shares that have some input into the job creation activity of Canada and there has been a risk taken, then there is some justification. My friend from Bird's Hill will agree there is some justification for giving a bit of a break.
But surely if one just buys a piece of land and it goes up in value, that is a different matter. There is no gain. No jobs are created. There is nothing done there. There might possibly be a job for the lawyer handling the purchase, possibly a job for the lawyer handling the sale and possibly a job for the real estate agent, but there is really nothing that makes Canada grow. It is a static investment.

March 30, 1993
Government Orders
My friend from London though is speaking of the small investment like the duplex or the store, something of that nature. He will know that under the other provisions of the Income Tax Act capital cost allowances, mortgages and all the rest of it are deductible from the earnings of those businesses to the extent that an income can be made, losses can be claimed and tax is not paid on the losses. There is a profit in that business, albeit small, but it is a profitable business.
That type of business is a business purchased for that reason and when the assets are sold gains tax should be paid on it. If it is incorporated, gains tax is paid. If it is held as an unincorporated amount then the $100,000 has previously been allowed. But surely that $100,000 exemption ought not to be allowed here because the property only goes up in value by the speculative increase in the market, not by anything that is done to the property to make it go up in value.
Real estate is different from investing in stocks or shares in a market oriented company. In a market oriented company shares can go up in value because the company produces profits. It moves ahead. The company retains growth because it does not distribute its earnings to its shareholders but retains those earnings. The company ploughs those earnings back in and it makes things grow.
Real estate is not like that. You buy a duplex and you rent it out. You maintain it presumably, but it does not grow in value. It may increase in value because of the general inflation in the area, but it does not grow in value by the work, the effort, the energy of the company like a stock does. It grows in value only for one reason. That is because of inflation and that is because the location may be more desirable.

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, March 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mulroney that Bill C-116, an act to provide for greater certainty in the reconciliation of the personal interests and duties of office of public office holders, to establish a Conflict of Interests Commission, to amend the Parliament of Canada Act and to make consequential amendments to other acts, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee in the Departmental envelope.

subtopic: CONFLICT OF INTERESTS OF PUBLIC OFFICE HOLDERS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to say a few things about Bill C-116.1 served on the joint committee that looked at Bill C-43, which was the previous bill introduced by the government to deal with conflicts of interest as it applies to members of Parliament and ministers.
Let me start by saying that the House of Commons represents the people of Canada. Those who are elected to the House of Commons do so through a process which involves their political parties. In the case of independent members, the independent will go directly to the constituents.
I want to stress that at no time has it been my experience that the people in any riding across this country have ever put a gun to the head of an individual and said: "You must run''. I have never known of anyone, and it is not in the historical experience of this House that any individual was ever forced to be a cabinet minister.
No one is forced to seek office in the House of Commons. In fact, in order to come here candidates actually court the electorate in elections. Therefore it is at the disposition of the electorate that we sit in this House. It is at the behest of the people of Canada that we are elected. It is a privilege for us to be here representing the people of our country and, in my case, the people of Nickel Belt.
March 30, 1993

I want to say that because when we deal with conflict of interest we have to recognize there is a tendency and temptation to suddenly become very righteous once we become members of Parliament.
When we are running for office it is not unknown to have a family portrait and to include the dog in the family picture. They say every politician should have a dog. They try to portray themselves as wonderful family persons.
Candidates do that. They are very open when they are running for office. They will tell anything about themselves. They will tell how many times they smoked paper and inhaled it. One of them said: "I smoked paper, but I did not inhale it". The other one said: "I did. I cannot tell a lie. I enjoyed it". They are very open, want to disclose everything. Nobody asked them to and they are willing to disclose.
It is positively indecent. Some of them should be arrested and charged with exposing all these things that one would consider before they sought office as private. Sorry, it is a family show.
They are elected to the House of Commons and suddenly the curtain of secrecy descends. No more willingness to disclose. The prevailing principle is for me to know and for the public to find out. That is the prevailing principle once elected to the House, and when they get into the cabinet do they ever do things.
We had one fellow here. He put all his holdings into a blind trust. The only problem was the blind trust was his wife. That was permissible. I know love is blind, but how can a blind trust be blind when you sleep with the same person who holds your blind trust.

subtopic: CONFLICT OF INTERESTS OF PUBLIC OFFICE HOLDERS ACT
speechtext: As long as the lights are out.

subtopic: CONFLICT OF INTERESTS OF PUBLIC OFFICE HOLDERS ACT
speechtext:
No, I am sorry, that is not true. No, it is not true. The hon. member said that we are all a bunch of crooks. No, it is not to say that. How was it when we were running for office we were so willing to disclose. Now we are elected and suddenly a curtain of secrecy has descended.
I want to put the Prime Minister on the record. In 1987 the Prime Minister warned would-be MPs, those who would be MPs: "You had better be ready to open your life and books to the public. We are going to be as
Government Orders
clear-cut and brutal as we can". That was the Prime Minister. He established a very high standard. Then we got Bill C-46 and before it we got Bill C-114. Then we got Bill C-43 and now we have Bill C-116.
There is no doubt being in the House of Commons, being a minister of the Crown, being a parliamentary secretary, that on occasions conflicts will arise. We recognize that, but the question then has to be asked: How do we deal with situations (a) to avoid the perception of conflict and (b) when there is a conflict how do we deal with it? It is where the private interests of the member interfaces with the public interest. When there is a conflict it must be resolved in the public interest. It means that we must put in place a regime to avoid as much as possible the possibility of conflicts arising.
The government once again in the dying days of a Parliament introduced Bill C-43. A joint committee was struck to look at that bill and it was lead by the member for Mississauga South as one of its co-chairpersons.
When we started out it was very interesting. There were members on the committee who subscribed to Mitchell Sharp's position that we should return to the era of C. D. Howe. It was a kinder, gentler era. Nobody accused C. D. Howe of having a potential or possible conflict when every day while he was a minister of the Crown he would take out his stocks and bonds and see how they were doing on the market at the same time he was minister for everything in the government.
There are members sitting in the House who subscribed to that, but to give them credit and to salute them I want to say that as we proceeded through the witnesses there was a very perceptible change. There was agreement that we could do better than Bill C-43. We came to an agreement and submitted our report to the government which was in effect a rewriting of the bill.
To start we did not see two regimes in the House of Commons. We did not see two regimes for resolving conflicts of interest. We did not see two regimes for reporting assets and liabilities of members. We saw what? We recommended a jurisconsult and that all members be subject to the jurisconsult. We would have one set of rules that applied to all members, parliamentary secretaries and ministers. We felt that was the way to provide some uniformity in the rules.

March 30, 1993
Government Orders
What have we discovered in the creation of Bill C-116? We see the creation of two bureaucracies, a bureaucracy called the commission with a commissioner for ministers, parliamentary secretaries and public servants, and for the ordinary garden-type member of Parliament, a jurisconsult.
There is a problem here. This is the Siamese twins of conflict of interest except they are not joined at the head. They are joined at some other part of the anatomy because from time to time there is an overlap. From time to time a minister would have to consult with the jurisconsult, not with the commission or the commissioner.
This would be creating a conflict of jurisdiction. The bill as we know it is riddled with terminological conflicts and definitions that do not mean the same thing to the two bureaucracies. For example, we had the minister check to see if he had a possible conflict of interest when an issue comes up in cabinet or within his jurisdiction. He then comes to the jurisconsult. He does not go to the commission.
How would the jurisconsult know if the minister has a conflict when the minister did not declare his assets and liabilities to the jurisconsult? He declared them to the commission. He has a problem.
The committee did not recommend that. We also have a problem with the question of recusal. The committee recognized that we should create the atmosphere in which the public has the assurance that we are acting in the spirit of the legislation which is the avoidance of a conflict or of the appearance of a conflict.
I will use these interchangeably because when Justice Parker looked at the Sinclair Stevens case he said even if there is an appearance of conflict there is conflict. In other words, if there is smoke there has to be fire.
Therefore on the question of recusal it is very important to honour the spirit of any conflict of interest law, the spirit of trying, attempting and satisfying the public that the public office holder has attempted to avoid the appearance of conflict.
Recusal means that if an issue comes up in committee, in the House or in the cabinet, a member may have a
conflict because for example we are dealing with the Bank Act and he owns more than one-third or 10 per cent of a bank. He then has to declare the interest. He has to declare the conflict. He has to remove himself or herself from the discussion of that particular change to the Bank Act and avoid voting on the issue.
It is not difficult. When I was a municipal councillor I did it. It is incumbent upon municipal councillors all across this country when an issue comes up to declare a conflict and remove themselves from debate and voting on that issue.
We recommended recusal for members and for ministers. We do not know what is going to happen behind the curtains of secrecy that shroud the class of ministers, public servants and parliamentary secretaries. We know for ordinary members there is no requirement for recusal.
It is interesting to note that in the conflict of interest laws in the United States, Ontario, Manitoba, la belle province and in many other jurisdictions, there is requirement for recusal. When a matter comes up where there is a conflict between a minister and the issue, between the member and the issue, that minister, that member, that parliamentary secretary, that public servant must recuse, must declare the interest and remove themselves. We do not have that in Bill C-116.
When we drafted our recommendations for the government we were even-handed in the way we treated those who held cabinet positions and those who were ordinary garden-fry type MPs. In this bill, it seems to be tougher for the MPs than the ministers, the parliamentary secretaries and the public servants. Let me explain what I am talking about. It is the question of disclosure.
Justice Parker said in his report on the Sinclair Stevens affair that full disclosure is the cornerstone on which any modern conflict of interest bill is built.
When we did our report on Bill C-43, the member for Mississauga South will remember we wanted disclosure and everybody treated the same. In Bill C-116 ministers, parliamentary secretaries and public servants will report to the commission. We do not know what they will report. It is not spelled out in the bill. Then the commission will draw up a summary and it may or may not be available for public scrutiny.
March 30, 1993

On the other hand, it specifies what the disclosure is going to be for the members. Certainly we never envisaged anything other than those assets that are purely personal. Justice Parker recommended that personal things such as your mortgage, RRSP funds and car loan ought to be excluded from disclosure. That is in line with what Justice Parker recommended with respect to the Sinclair Stevens affair.
When it came to spouses, there was a co-extensive disclosure for spouses of MPs.
