In all fairness to my friend and colleague, I will make sure I do not use all my time so one of the senior members can participate in the debate. I am referring to the hon. member for Annapolis Valley-Hants, a good friend.
It is a conflict of interest because I have known his father for so many years that I owe it to him to give him some time during the debate. I do not want to make any comments. I would just like to participate in the debate.

I sat on that committee, which I consider to be a very important one. For the sake of our listeners, perhaps I should explain what we mean by committee. It is a place where members can work in peace and quiet, or at least in as much peace and quiet as they can muster, on very important legislation. For instance, I am now on the electoral reform committee, which has been sitting for hundreds of hours so far. This kind of thing does not make the headlines. It is a serious business and it is the same kind of work we did when a government bill, Bill
Government Orders
C-43, was submitted to us on December 12, 1991. In any case our first meeting was held on that date.
We met 26 times. We examined the bill and called experts who appeared before the committee for long hours at a time. We met witnesses, dozens of them, and I may add that one of the members of our committee who did excellent work was the newly elected Premier of Prince Edward Island. Yes, Ms. Callbeck, my colleague, was a member of this joint committee of the Senate and the House of Commons.
Perhaps I should explain as well that in French comite mixte does not mean a committee consisting of men and women, but of senators and members of the House of Commons. There are several senators and several members of the House of Commons, and one of those members was Ms. Callbeck who finished her work on the committee and who yesterday was elected Premier of Prince Edward Island. I am sure all my colleagues will want to congratulate her.

As I was saying, Ms. Callbeck, a lady of great experience was elected premier of Prince Edward Island yesterday. I am sure the co-chair, the hon. member for Mississauga South and the hon. Senator Stanbury will join with me in giving her our best wishes.

I explained more or less what a joint committee is and what a committee does, which is serious business, unlike the circus we often see in the House, which tends to give Canadians a poor impression of the kind of work federal members of Parliament do, five days a week and almost ten months a year. Now our sitting days have been shortened, but we are still sitting five days a week. That compares very favourably with the schedule of provincial legislatures.
We sat on this committee because we felt it was not any easier to legislate the honesty of parliamentarians than to legislate morality. Since some people, as soon as they see members in a position of strength-and even more so in the case of senators, ministers and parliamentary secretaries-imagine that all these people are there to get rich. We had to restore public confidence through legislation. These bills will not eliminate the problem

March 30,1993
Government Orders
altogether, however, and the public has a responsibility to remain vigilant.
As I have always said, the national media have a watchdog role. They must ensure that parliamentarians do what they were elected to do: pass good bills for the people of this country, although occasionally they maybe tough, and that they do not in any way take advantage of their position to increase their personal wealth or that of their spouse or dependents.
I have seen quite a bit in the course of my political career, and I must say I feel uncomfortable, as a member of this committee, drafting a bill that says that from now on there will be fewer temptations. The temptations will always be there. But who often puts us in that kind of position? The people who hope that we can use our position to fill their pockets.
This bill is not perfect. I must make that clear. It is our fourth try. The hon. member for Sudbury and the hon. member for Nickel Belt, from northern Ontario have pointed out there had been another bill before. For those who are interested in that sort of thing, we had Bill C-46, Bill C-114 and Bill C-43, which we examined and scrutinized and on which we made some major recommendations to the House. The government based Bill C-116, the bill we are considering today, on this report by the parliamentary committee of the Senate and the House of Commons.
I support this bill. Whenever I travel abroad on official duties and have a few hours of free time I take advantage of that time to study, for instance, the question we are talking about today, the conflict of interest legislation. On another occasion it might be the Canada Elections Act, since my whip appointed me to that committee as well and I have a special interest in the matter. There is also the matter of parliamentary associations, because I am a firm believer in the principle that parliamentarians should know what is going on in the world. So at no cost to the state I use my free time, rather than for shopping or sightseeing, to visit different legislatures in the world where my duty calls me and to study them.
In Australia, I discovered a simple bill. I am one of those who want this bill to be clear, simple and straightforward, so that people can understand it on first
reading, take it in and say, "I am satisified; it is reasonably acceptable."
That is why Australia, for example, has a bill requiring all parliamentarians to own up. After they have confessed in private, the official in charge, called a jurisconsult or commissioner, tables in Parliament in the usual way the potential conflicts of interest that parliamentarians may have so that the public and the press can be aware of them.
I have never believed and never will believe that we shoul qualitatively describe any fortune parliamentarians might have or put figures on it that would unduly excite people who might make comparisons like "my MP is richer than another" or "my senator is richer than someone else". I do not think that is what the people want to know. People want to know about any apparent conflicts of interest.
What we are doing is distinguishing between the quantitative and qualitative aspects. It is unnecessary for the public to know the exact figures, but it is very important for the commissioner and the jurisconsult to know exactly what a member might have and what he or she might owe, because debts are always dangerous; they can lead to conflicts of interest.
In an ideal world, it would be better not to have such legislation, and I am very conservative on this subject. Unfortunate incidents have occurred, but in spite of everything, I still say how proud I am to be a parliamentarian. When people ask what I do, I do not hide that I am a member of Parliament. I do not have to apologize. I am not ashamed because some Canadians these days are annoyed with us. They have to take it out on somebody and they go after the most important institution, in my opinion, the parliamentary system. That is bad. Just because unemployment is too high or people are unhappy about inflation, the sales tax, some government policies or certain leaders, does not mean that they have to take it out on the system which governs us. It is still a good system. I often regret that people get it all confused and destroy the credibility of the parliamentary system.
I urge my colleagues, in a non-partisan way, to read yesterday's Hansard because I find that it summarizes our thinking very well. For members and other people who want to read it, it is Issue No. 229 of Hansard for Monday, March 29. I would like them to read the excellent presentation made by our committee chairman, the member for Mississauga South, and the statement of
March 30, 1993

Government Orders
my friend and colleague, the member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell, who was very generous to me in mentioning my work on the committee. Of course the press does not know about it because we sit quietly without making a noise. As you know, making noise does not always do the most good. Those who shout the loudest are not necessarily right. I also suggest that they read the remarkable presentation of the hon. member for Oshawa. I think that those three speeches yesterday summarize very well the work that was done.
We have concerns, we hope and believe the time will come to consider in committee.

I hope the House will accept the recommendation of our able chairman, the member for Mississauga South, and create a special committee of both Houses, the Senate and the House of Commons. We worked together for a long time and produced a report. The report gave birth to Bill C-116. It has a long title. I am told it could be shorter by saying it is a bill that will try to avoid conflict of interest of ministers, parliamentary secretaries and hon. senators in one group and elected members of Parliament who are not in responsible positions in another.
I hope the government will still be open to polishing it up at the committee level. I see our chairman, the hon. member for Mississauga South and hon. Senator Stanbu-ry, the co-chair. It is not always easy to work with the chairman but it is very exciting to be a member of any committee he chairs. He is a tough man but some of us are equally tough and can endure it. I wish to thank him for the good job he did. He sometimes tried to stampede us, but those who like to be stampeded are just stampeded and those who can resist do resist. I hope to qualify in the last category.
I would like to take two more minutes to make something clear in the minds of the press and the people. The press is the intermediary in our parliamentary system, the power of the people. You have to understand that my colleague and I do not want to put the members of Parliament above the law. It has nothing to do with that.

As the member for Oshawa said so well yesterday, and you should read what he said, members of Parliament must not be above the law for anything of a criminal nature. I would never support a bill that would treat us differently from the rest of the population in criminal matters. If any of us commits a crime, the law is there to come down as hard, not necessarily harder, but as hard as for any crime someone might commit.
This is a special situation here, because we are elected members of Parliament or senators. Some members, because of their position as a minister or parliamentary secretary, might hear some things or see some documents or be able to use confidential information that they obtained through their position here in Parliament. This bill is to ensure that these people do not profit unduly to enrich themselves or their family and friends. Naturally it is called the Conflict of Interests Act.
I am very serious when I say that I do not like to hear about all those wonderful laws in the United States, as my committee chairman knows. I get annoyed every time I hear about them. I say: "Please do not talk to me about a system that may not be the best example in the world to follow". If anyone has conflicts of interest it is our southern neighbours. I do not like comparisons about the Elections Act, campaign spending limits and especially the famous conflict of interests legislation. I have the feeling that they always have conflicts of interest, so I do not like the comparison. I want something that is essentially Canadian and draws on the best of other political systems in the world. Then I think we can honestly come back to the House and say that we have done our duty in an honest way and produced a bill that will be revised over the years.
I admit that what we will produce is better than what exists. I admit that what we will produce will not be as good as what our successors can do. But it is a start in the right direction and I hope that people will stop being cynical about politicians because, after all, we were all elected from various political parties by the people and the time is coming when you will again be able to choose your representatives. I would like this bill to be implemented and I hope that we do not give up this work.

March 30,1993
Government Orders

I hope the chairman will be tough if he is chairman again and he should be chairman again. He should be tough to make sure this law becomes law before the end of this Parliament.

In conclusion, we have an excellent system in Quebec to deal with conflicts of interest.
Again, I say in all modesty that what we are proposing is a good imitation of what the provinces are doing. We are suggesting a jurisconsult, just as the Quebec National Assembly has, and a commissioner, like Mr. Evans in Ontario. I want to pay tribute to him and to Mr. Justice Mayrand as well. They are above suspicion. I think that is the key to success in applying this law. The first jurisconsult to be chosen, who will become an officer of the House of Commons, should be above suspicion and earn the immediate confidence of the public. That will be a good beginning.
In the parliamentary committee and in my first speech I suggested having someone with the reputation of Mr. Justice Mayrand or Malouf or former senior officials of the Department of Justice who, once they are appointed, will inspire the confidence that the public is asking or seeking from Parliament.
I hope that the commissioner who will be chosen-and I will have some suggestions to make about that-will be above suspicion. I hope that the system will be administered impartially, in the same way for all. I am not too fond of the dichotomy which seems to come out of this bill, but I really hope that when we review it we can make improvements and the government will agree to receive amendments.

subtopic: CONFLICT OF INTERESTS OF PUBLIC OFFICE HOLDERS ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too want to share in some of the thoughts expressed here earlier. Certainly I can relieve the anxiety of the hon. member for Saint-Denis, who is one of the more venerable members and certainly second to the dean of the House. I was interested in his comments.
I think part of my problem with this bill is that my colleague and I have been here a few years and came in under totally different regimes when there was certainly a different reflection of the public will on the thoughts of members. I will come to that later. The hon. member complimented the co-chair of the joint committee that produced a unanimous report earlier on Bill C-43. Then the government came up with this bill which is a blend of aspects of Bill C-43 dealing with public office holders and another part in Bill C-116, which we are now dealing with, which affects members of Parliament.
The hon. member for Saint-Denis was hoping the chairman and government would not move so quickly. I know the issue of conflict of interest has been around for a long time. The public feels there is a fundamental flaw in the whole system because somehow members and/or ministers have got in trouble, as they have historically since Confederation in this jurisdiction and other jurisdictions across the way. As members have said before me "you cannot legislate all the time to cover the sometimes innate sin and guilt of mankind" although churches preach about it often on Sundays across the nation. But that does not mean we do not need a conflict of interest law in terms of public office holders.
It has not been mentioned here today that the Parliament of Canada Act has a section which deals with members of Parliament who may not vote on matters where they are personally going to benefit. They have to declare their interest and/or abstain. This comes from the British mother of Parliament system. That seems to work over there and it works pretty darned well. There is a character and integrity involved that somehow we as a younger country have not quite inherited.
The member for Mississauga South showed very interesting parliamentary diligence when he had the House agree unanimously yesterday to a motion on Bill C-116, which just came on the floor of the House yesterday afternoon at 4.10 p.m. and the House adjourned at 5.28, that between 1 and 1.55 today all debate and matters are to be disposed of in terms of Bill C-116, which affects every member of Parliament and every senator. The Senate will have its time, of course, to debate it.
In effect, as I compute the matter in old-fashioned arithmetic and not the computer, that is one hour and
March 30, 1993

eighteen minutes yesterday and 55 minutes today for a total of just two hours and a few minutes on a bill that affects us all.
I agree with the member for Saint-Denis. I hope all members and/or the secretaries who may be tuned in to this television look at the debate yesterday on the generalities developed by the hon. member for Mississauga South and the spokespersons for the opposition, the member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell and the spokesperson for the NDP, the member for Oshawa, who taunt the generalities.
I hope members will go further so when this matter gets to a committee, be it a joint or whatever, they look at a document I got out of the library prepared by Margaret Young of the Law and Government Division of the Research Branch of the Parliament of Canada. It is a legislative summary of this bill and she covers the generalities well. There are many good works done in the Research Branch of Parliament. I commend this 31-page document that reviews the general problems of this issue of balancing public duty with the privacy of the person when you are in the public domain.
I know the potential co-chair of the committee touched on the issues in a very general way in his comments yesterday, but this document deals with many specifics, some of which put a higher onus on the member than the office holder. The old C-43 was drafted onto the new 116, and there are some elements in there which I think all members would be concerned about. I certainly hope the committee knows that the member from Mississauga South shows interest in this and he has been at this for some time. He will look closely at this legislative review done by our impartial library and hopefully redress some problems there that I think even he may be unaware of at the present time.
I know the member for Mississauga South, under the rule, has a motion to help move this along. All members want this moved along, but quite frankly there can be a delusion in this conflict of interest bill. Fundamental good work is not developed in members if there is some cancer in their moral id that is going to permeate their public business. You can have all the rules and regulations you want.
I have been in this Chamber for over 25 years and you can pervert or prostitute any rule of procedure and/or
Government Orders
almost any rule or regulation that is not in the criminal domain unless you have some character, integrity or common good sense. I have heard what the members have said here and I know the members spent a lot of time on this in the committee, but we are developing two parallel bureaucracies that the member for Saint-Denis touched upon, to try to define the ethics and morals that members are supposed to follow. We are doing this in reaction to the public and/or media negative element that has cast a cloud over members of this House.
I am not going to get political, but in my 25 plus years as a member of Parliament, I honestly do not know where I have run into a potential conflict of interest. I would like to know from the member for Nickel Belt, as a member of Parliament, what conflict he has run into in discharging his duty. The member for Mississauga South is a lawyer and has business interests. I still would venture that he has not run into potential conflicts but one is never to ask a question unless one knows the answer so I am only asking rhetorically at the present time.
The point is that the tone and the climate of the House of Commons and how members and the government discharge their duties is really set by the Prime Minister and/or the cabinet and there is a world of difference between a member of Parliament and a cabinet minister or a parliamentary secretary. Something that is not even covered in this bill is deputy ministers or heads of some of the important government agencies. These individuals along with deputy ministers and/or ministers and parliamentary secretaries do have information and do come across facts that could further their private interests.
I know this is perhaps not the politically correct thing and the member for Nickel Belt cast aspersions on this on another day when the Hon. Mitchell Sharp gave evidence before the committee. I was in this House of Commons when the Hon. Mitchell Sharp was not only the then Liberal government House leader but he was the Minister of Finance. To me he was one of the more-and he still is because he is still very much alive and with it-honourable ones in the days when I used to believe that the Liberal government was infallible. The days of infallible Grit rule were forever because they had not been beaten for 20 or 30 years.

March 30, 1993
Government Orders
When I first came here as a young pup there they all were, not C. D. Howe, but Mr. Pearson, Mr. Sharp, Mr. Winters and many others. They were all fine Canadians. I do not know what happened then but the element of conflict of interest did not seem to make all the headlines because the Prime Minister of the day and the cabinet of the day stayed out of trouble. Even then there is a world of difference between cabinet members and their responsibility and their potential power of advancing themselves with confidential information over the rest of this House.
I will read in effect what Mr. Sharp said among other things before the committee: "I was a senior civil servant for 16 years and privy to inside information from which I could have benefited if I had put my private interests ahead of my public responsibility. For another 13 years, I was a minister of the Crown. Again I was an insider making decisions and aware of decisions being made collectively by the cabinet from which I could have benefited if I had put my private interests ahead of my public responsibilities. For a couple of years after I left cabinet in 1976, and before I resigned my seat in 1978,1 was generally regarded as an ordinary MP. I was no longer an insider. I did not have access to any information on future government decisions from which I could have profited that was not publicly available."
I will just conclude this part of what I want to say. What Mr. Sharp said before the committee with his vast experience both as a distinguished public servant, a very distinguished minister of the Crown and then in effect a backbencher before he got out of the whole business was that there was in effect a world of difference. What we know here we find out almost the same way as when he says one reads it in the paper or hears it over the news.
That is one of the philosophical problems I have with equating this even in the one bill. I know there are two regimes. Perhaps there should be two bills, one to look after ministers, parliamentary secretaries and public office holders, including deputy ministers and heads of government organizations, and then one for the members and senators who do not have the same access to information to in effect have the conflict.
The other element of the bill that I really seriously hope the committee takes a very close look at in the closing two minutes I have is the whole question of the spousal declaration of her or his interests. I know they
have wrestled with this. I am still unsatisfied with the way this bill is. It just boggles the mind on this International Day of the Woman or International Year of the Woman and all this advancement quite properly of the woman to make that person equal in society in every which way, that we are going to put into a bill a part that says that in effect a member can do what he wants to do but if the member is a man then his wife must disclose whatever interests she may or may not have.
Mr. Speaker, as you well know, there is a reverse side to this that organizers getting ready for the next election might run into. We all know that there are a lot more women who should be in this House. You are going to have the interesting situation in effect of campaign organizers going to the woman of very eminent Canadians who may have business interests to ask them to run.
Some parties have quotas. They want 25 per cent or 50 per cent as women. They go to that lady and they say: "Mrs. Brown you have to run for us". She talks to her husband over supper that night and Mr. Brown says: "Well, Matilda, I would like you to be a member of Parliament but there is no way. You do not know what I do. You know I am a big business man. You have not seen my books. You do not know what my finances are. You do not know that I may be in a state of personal bankruptcy that I do not really want to tell my competitors about. I would rather that you would not run. I do not understand why as a member your declaration that you are not going to commit any crime or have a conflict of interest should affect me".
I seriously hope that the committee gets to this. I could give many chapters and verses of how this is a complete negative reaction to what we have tried to do here to make the genders equal. Here we are putting them right back in the Dark Ages with this type of regime.

speechtext: It being two o'clock p.m. we shall proceed to statements by members.

Mr. Speaker, in 1986 the Deschenes commission recommended the Criminal Code be amended to allow for the prosecution of war criminals.
I sat on the committee for Bill C-71, which led to the establishment of the war crimes investigation unit, and I looked forward to justice finally being served.

March 30,1993
I am sorry to report more than six years later that although 300 people are under active investigation not one person has yet been convicted for crimes committed.
Today a delegation from the Jewish Students' Network is meeting here in Ottawa to discuss the government's commitment to pursuing war criminals and bringing them to justice. We would do well to emulate the dedication of these young people in their determination to ensure Canada is not a safe haven for war criminals. The wheels of justice must move faster.
We owe those who died in the Holocaust and the families and friends who survived to pursue the perpetrators of these heinous crimes. We must not forget.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgency. The lobster industry in southern Nova Scotia at the height of the season suffered the worst damage to gear since 1976 as a result of the storm of the century two weeks ago. As a result of the winter weather assessment of damage by the fishermen has been difficult.
I met with close to 50 fishermen in Yarmouth last Saturday. I have received 73 assessments of damages totalling $850,000 from Shelburne to Digby counties, and I am sure that there are many more.
The minister of fisheries has in the past provided assistance to fishermen: the weir fishermen in the Bay of Fundy, assistance for gearing up in the northern cod and lobster fishermen in P.E.I.
With more than two months to fish the lobster fishermen in southern Nova Scotia find themselves with reduced gear. These fishermen need help today. I call on the minister of fisheries to provide assistance so that they will not suffer more financial losses by not being able to go lobster fishing.

Mr. Speaker, today I would like to commend the efforts of the Dugald Costume Museum, which is now celebrating its 10th anniversary.
The 10th anniversary is a little misleading in that this volunteer group actually started over 40 years ago. Its desire to preserve and display different types of clothing is unique and is also world leading in concept. The 15,000 volunteer hours annually demonstrate the depth and conviction of this community-based group.
I would like to invite all members of the House to visit the museum's 10th anniversary display, "Let's Dance". I know the time spent will be most enjoyable.

Mr. Speaker, in 1870 the Americans prevented the Canadian ship Chico-ra from entering into Lake Superior through their lock system.
An 1871 article in the Toronto Globe stated: "It is quite plain-that the Dominion of Canada cannot allow the Americans to have exclusive control of the means of water communication between Lakes Huron and Superior".
Thus a $4 million Canadian Sault Canal was built in 1895. Owing to a structural failure the canal has been closed to navigation since 1987. Attempts at obtaining funds for its restoration have been difficult.
However I am optimistic that a $5.9 million commitment from the Ontario NDP government, a commitment from the city of Sault Ste. Marie to do landscaping and road work and continued expressions of support from the Minister of Public Works could lead to the restoration of the lock.
Public Works has selected a recreational lock costing $11.75 million as its first choice option.
I call upon the Minister of the Environment to respond positively to this most significant initiative in Sault Ste. Marie.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Thursday I had the privilege of accompanying the Minister of Indian Affairs and the Minister of State for Transport to the launching ceremony of the $350,000 expansion of the Vancouver International Airport.
March 30,1993

The Vancouver International Airport Authority, a not for profit corporation which took over operations from the federal government last year, has developed plans to build a new international terminal building and a new runway, both to be completed by 1996.
Full consideration is being given to the environmental impact of construction and special efforts will be made on the issues of noise reduction, habitat preservation and the maintaining of green spaces.
In addition, the federal government, through Transport Canada, will complement these new facilities by constructing a new control tower and an instrument landing system at a cost of just over $20 million.
It should be noted that the airport authority has devised a method of paying for the runway and terminal building improvements without depending on government grants, subsidies or guarantees.
Congratulations to Chester Johnson, chairman of the airport authority; David Emerson, president and chief executive officer of the authority; and all of the other people who have contributed to these plans to prepare Vancouver International Airport for the 21st century.

Mr. Speaker, today I would like to congratulate members of Network Canada, an organization of Jewish young people who are here today to tell us about their fight against hate crimes and their concern about the growing number of groups that promote hate.

According to Klanwatch, an organization dedicated to monitoring racist groups, there are 46 known hate groups in our country. In fact their operations are so prevalent in Canada that Klanwatch dedicated an entire issue of its magazine to hate activities in our country.
Members of the network know that groups like White Aryan Resistance and the Klan are actively recruiting in our schools. We cannot sit back and do nothing.
It is about time that the new Minister of Justice and the Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship concentrate their efforts on finding an effective means of controlling hate groups and eliminating them from our society.

Mr. Speaker, on February 18, 1993 I asked the Speaker of the House of Commons to freeze my member's office budget. On February 22, 1993 I declared in Parliament that I had refused to accept the 3.16 per cent increase in my main budget for 1993-94.
Today, to my satisfaction, I received a reply from the House of Commons that should be welcomed by Canadian taxpayers. My budget has been frozen at its 1992-93 level. On behalf of my Abitibi constituents, I want to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for accepting my request, and I will maintain the same services.
In Bill C-113, the government decided to make cuts in a number of federal programs and freeze the salaries of certain groups.
Today, I urge my Conservative, Liberal, NDP and Bloc Quebecois colleagues to follow suit and help reduce government spending and the federal deficit.

Mr. Speaker, on March 27, 1993 I had the distinct honour of celebrating the 100th anniversary of Manotick Lodge 295 with members of the Independent Order of Odd Fellows.
It is with pleasure that I salute the present and past Grand Nobles, as well as their brothers and sisters of the Manotick Lodge, for their continued devotion in assisting their fellow persons in need.

March 30, 1993
The worthy causes they give aid to include the Os-goode Care Centre, the Canadian Guide Dog for the Blind, the Kars Fair Youth and the Arthritis Association, just to name a few.
I commend the Independent Order of Odd Fellows for giving its best efforts to the needy of the community. Odd Fellows of Manotick, thank you.

Mr. Speaker, if there is still any question about how the people of Prince Edward Island feel about the fixed link there was a very clear answer in yesterday's provincial election.
Ninety-five per cent of voters voted for parties in favour of the fixed link. Five per cent voted for the one party against the project. That is 95 to 5 in favour of the project.
Obviously, there were many other issues involved in the vote, but if there existed strong opposition yesterday was the opportunity for people to register their concerns or even stop the project.
During our legislative committee deliberations witnesses indicated that support for the link was growing. Yesterday's election seems to support that position.
With this clear message I again urge the government to make a determination under the recent court decision and proceed with the project.

Mr. Speaker, you will remember that two weeks ago I entered my horse Slip Chaser into the Tory leadership stakes to be run in June.
Last Friday at the London fairgrounds Slip Chaser held a press conference to declare that he has been eating grass since he was bom three years ago and he enjoys it, but he cannot understand why anyone would smoke it. He questioned his opponent's judgment about something so basic and suggested that delegates ought to seriously consider a candidate who knows what grass is for.
As for the GST, Slip Chaser declared it to be discrimi-natoiy on the grounds that it exempts medical services to humans but not horses. He would therefore abolish it.
In response to a question from reporters about his chances of winning the Tory leadership race Slip Chaser replied: "Given the opportunity to vote for the whole horse, I am confident that Tory delegates will elect me Prime Minister, the first whole horse to occupy the position".

subtopic: CANADIAN NATIONAL INSTITUTE FOR THE BLIND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to join today with people from across Canada in commemoration of the 75th anniversary of the Canadian National Institute for the Blind.
Since 1918 the CNIB has been providing services to the blind and the visually impaired to ensure that they can be meaningful and contributing members of our society. Disability should be no limitation and the CNIB has led the way.
This morning in St. John's, Newfoundland some 400 people came together to celebrate the 75th anniversary of the CNIB. I know that all members of the House would want to join with them.

Mr. Speaker, while the UN gambles on the possibility of a negotiated settlement in the former Yugoslavia more than 120,000 people have been murdered and 20,000 women have been raped, some as young as four years old.
The confession of a Serbian soldier describes one of the 20,000 rapes. He said: "What I remember about the first woman I raped was that she was pretty. I only remember some of their names. Fatima was a nice woman. After raping her, I took her at gunpoint to the mountains. I stopped by a small bridge and I told her to get out. She walked about three metres away from the car and I just shot her. My commander told me it was good for morale to rape and kill Bosnian women".
This account is horrific. As a leader in the international community the Canadian government has a moral obligation to do more than just condemn these barbaric
March 30,1993

acts, it must lead in forcing the United Nations to take all steps necessary to stop these atrocities.
Why does this Parliament justify its silence by pointing to sanctions which have been insufficient and a no-fly zone that goes unenforced? When women and children are being raped and murdered, why has Canada lost its courageous and leading voice on the international stage?
God and history will judge us all very harshly for inaction in this matter.

speakerposition: Chief Government Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to draw the attention of the House to the grave situation in war-tom former Yugoslavia.
For months now Bosnia-Hercegovina has been engaged in a bloody war, the details of which we are all unfortunately familiar with: the heinous ethnic cleansing, the rapes, the torture, the concentration camps, the famine and the wounded. The much vaunted sanctions seem to have no impact at all on the aggressor.
Canada has denounced the acts of violence and terror. We are providing peacekeeping troops and we are supplying emergency humanitarian relief.
Diplomatically, we have recognized the independence of Croatia, Slovenia and Bosnia-Hercegovina, and we believe that the people of the former republic of Macedonia have a legitimate claim to recognition.
At this time peace may be pending in Bosnia. The Muslim and Croat leaders have signed a UN-mediated peace plan, but the Bosnian Serb leader has not yet signed.
I suggest that the government's top priority should be to strengthen diplomatic relations with all peace-seeking parties and to further isolate the outstanding party in order to pressure the Bosnian Serb leader to sign.
Once peace has been achieved in the region then the Canadian government should establish diplomatic agencies in all recognized former republics.

Mr. Speaker, when members of Parliament read their mail they will be well aware that the health food community does not like what Health and Welfare Canada is doing.
Specifically, they do not like schedule 705 of the food and drug regulations which will arbitrarily remove 64 herbs and botanical foodstuffs from health food stores. They do not like the harmonization article of the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement, article 708, restricting the availability of herbs they have used safely for many years.
They especially do not like restricting these foodstuffs to prescription use only as their availability and price will be taken over by the multinational drug companies.
Multinational drug companies have dictated that generic drugs be eliminated and now they are taking control of herbs and botanical foodstuffs.

Mr. Speaker, leaders of Canada's Jewish community gather in Ottawa today to welcome Israel's Minister of Foreign Affairs, Shimon Perez, and to strengthen the ties between Israel and Canada.
Israel, a dream for over 2,000 years, became a reality only 45 years ago in the aftermath of the holocaust. Its transformation from an arid desert to an advanced nation, in spite of wars, non-recognition by neighbouring states and continuing hostilities, is testimony to the ingenuity and commitment of the Israeli people.
Canada must continue as an enthusiastic partner in Israel's future by expanding our ties of trade and investment, fostering human rights and development and condemning the Arab boycott of Israel. We must not tolerate hate literature, neo-Naziism or any form of racism, and continue to pursue and bring Nazi war criminals to justice in Canada.

March 30, 1993
Oral Questions
Above all else, a cornerstone of Canada's foreign policy must always be the security of Israel, the only democracy in the Middle East, and Canada's close ally and special friend.

Mr. Speaker, last Sunday, the Minister of Finance again told the country there was one deficit and one taxpayer, thus continuing his alarmist comments about the size of provincial deficits.

The minister will know that the $5.8 billion he is planning to spend on helicopters is enough to clear the deficit of his home province of Alberta with enough money to spare to write off the combined deficits of Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and P.E.I.
If there is one taxpayer and one debt, why is there still a big spender across the floor?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is somewhat misleading in her assertions.
She is suggesting some $5 billion-and I correct her, it is $4.4 billion-is going to be spent in one year. That is not true. It is $4.4 billion spread over 13 or 14 years of which there are significant and positive economic spinoffs, benefits and jobs for Canadians. Most important, it will allow our Canadian servicemen and women the kind of equipment they deserve to carry out their important duties and missions.

Mr. Speaker, the government would rather borrow money to buy its choppers than chop its borrowing.

I have a supplementary question. Bill C-91, the drug patent bill, will increase costs for provincial health plans, making it even harder for the provinces to cut costs as required by the minister.
Will the minister cover the additional costs arising from the drug patent extensions he is imposing on the provinces so that Canada can maintain the universality of its health care programs? Will he end the universal indifference of this government to Canadians?
Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health
and Welfare): Mr. Speaker, we have answered this kind of question many times before in this House.
The hon. member raises the issue of universality of health care programs. The government has never considered challenging the universality of medicare. On the contrary, I have stated many times that the government was standing by its commitments in this respect.
As usual the party opposite is trying to raise doubts in the minds of Canadians. However, I do not think the provinces or Canadians in general are concerned. This has no connection with Bill C-91, which was warmly received by Canada's research community, because it will finally give Canadians the ability to develop research skills, especially in the medical field, that will make it possible to keep Canadian researchers in this country. I believe that when you consider this aspect, Bill C-91 is well received by the country as a whole.
Mr. Speaker, the minister must take his advice from Aunt Jemima because he sure loves to waffle.
Oh, oh.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Employment and Immigration.
Recently published Immigration Canada statistics reveal that in 1991 this government brought into Canada 56,000 immigrants who are listed as having no intention of working in this country. At the same time many highly educated and motivated young applicants are still being routinely rejected.
I ask the minister why he continues to claim that thousands of jobs are left unfilled for lack of skilled applicants when his policy is to import record high numbers of people who want no job at all.
March 30, 1993

speakeroldname: Hon. Bernard Valcourt (Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, these are the very people who opposed the amendments we made to the Immigration Act in order to try to get into Canada the kind of people we need to help our economy. These people are talking about skills development yet they opposed Bill C-21, an act to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, which has seen the activation of a massive amount of money to train people to get jobs.
I think we are on the right track. I take her question as an admission that they were wrong all along.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Deputy Prime Minister.
This government is in the fifth year of what the Prime Minister has referred to on many occasions as a four-year mandate. Even before the tabling of the budget in the House of Commons the government says it has no money.
I want to ask the Deputy Prime Minister who is also the Minister of Finance why he is allowing his cabinet colleagues to hand out billions of dollars of contracts with the EH-101 helicopters, thereby committing future governments to these expenditures? Why is he doing that?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, talk about inconsistencies and contradictions. Every day members across the way get up in the House and ask us what we are going to do about jobs and the creation of new economic activity and employment.
Here is a classic example where we are not only going to improve our defence capability, but we are going to create jobs and economic spin-offs, skills in high tech and a world product mandate. Why is the hon. member arguing about that?

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I guess there will be lots of jobs for Tory lobbyists.

I have a supplementary question for the Minister of Finance. A number of leadership candidates in his own
Oral Questions
party want the EH-101 helicopter contract cancelled. I would like to ask the Minister of Finance whether today he is prepared to announce a moratorium on all new contracts for EH-101 helicopters, as requested by a number of his own colleagues.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I made my position abundantly clear in the House on Friday, yesterday, today, and I will make it again right now.

Mr. Speaker, several groups representing rural Saskatchewan are in Ottawa today. They have brought concerns and frustrations that are reflected by all rural Canadians.
Despite the fact that the federal government has spent $12 billion to $15 billion in agriculture in the past eight years, 1,500 farmers are leaving the farm in Saskatchewan alone every year. The average farm income is expected to fall to about $5,000, a level not seen since the 1930s. Whether it be cuts to the Canadian Wheat Board or unilateral cuts to the Crow benefit, this government's programs have failed. Rural Canadians should be upset, urban Canadians should be upset and taxpayers should be upset.
I ask the agriculture minister: is the government planning to change its course? What plan does it have to bring about a new approach to developing programs that will bring hope instead of misery to Canadian farm families and to rural communities?

Mr. Speaker, I had a chance to attend not all but most of the submissions this morning. There is no question that there is a serious problem in Saskatchewan. I was impressed with the tone and some of the substance of the submissions. People were saying that they want to solve their problem within their fiscal means. There was a willingness to work together and to take a look at improving farm programs that we have. We have always taken that position as a federal government.
People were suggesting that they needed more education and more real training. I think over all there is a general recognition that no one group, whether it be

March 30, 1993
Oral Questions
federal or provincial governments or the producers by themselves, can do it all by themselves. That is the tone and that is the approach we have taken in this government to try to address this problem. That is the approach that we will continue to take, to work with many of the groups that appeared this morning before the Standing Committee on Agriculture.

Mr. Speaker, one of the things that these groups all called for was co-operation. One of the things that groups from the western Canadian wheat growers to the National Farmers Union called upon was the need for a third line of defence payment. In fact this government once promised Canadian farmers that if a crisis developed in farming it would bring in a third line of defence payment to help farmers in crisis.
We need long-term programs to help farms and rural communities. We have to keep those farms and those rural communities around until such programs can be put in place.
I would like to ask the Minister of Agriculture if he plans to announce today whether he is planning to bring in a third line of defence payment for Canadian farmers now.

Mr. Speaker, as I said, there is no question that there is a need. But we are not going to solve the problem, and I think it came out this morning in committee, simply by throwing money at it. Some of the witnesses made that almost as a direct observation.
I say again, we want to continue to work with people. I would suggest that he encourage the government of Saskatchewan, his province, to work with the federal government to see if we can develop better financial assistance for farmers, better over-all security programs for income.
I do not think it is useful in Saskatchewan simply to stand up as a provincial government and say that the GRIP program is flawed and withdraw from it without coming forward with some ideas on how we can make it better.
We are going to try very hard to work with the Government of Saskatchewan. In the meantime, we
should take some hints from what was said this morning at committee and realize that we have to work together and that there is a limit to the amount of money with which we have to work.

Mr. Speaker, since the minister is having great difficulty coming to grips with the third line of defence payment program, I wonder if he would reconsider some of the policies the government has announced recently. Would he agree to defer the 10 per cent cut to transport payments to railways, which means the farmer has to pay over $2 a tonne extra this coming year? Would he increase the initial prices, which was one of the proposals that was put in front of the meeting this morning? Also, will he promise to continue with interest-free cash advances, something that his government cancelled two or three years ago?

Mr. Speaker, as a farmer the hon. member should know better than to make the last statement. Cash advances are still in effect for farmers. They were put in late. To listen to that member you would think that in fact they were cancelled, when in fact he knows better than that. He knows they were not.
They are not in legislation. One year at a time.

He wants to yell from his seat, Mr. Speaker.
With regard to initial payments, we are always willing to look at increasing initial payments. We have done it twice already this year. We said from the beginning when we formed the government over eight years ago that that was an ongoing policy. We will continue to do that.
He also talked about other things. Just let me say again that if he wants to make representations to the federal government he should go to his own province. Witnesses this morning said that the changes that were made in the Saskatchewan GRIP cost Saskatchewan producers something like $200 million to $300 million. If he wants to make representations to the federal government he should do it through his own ilk in Saskatchewan and see if he can get some results there.

The same question on the same subject to the same minister, Mr. Speaker.
March 30, 1993

Members of this House learned this morning about the severe plight of many prairie grain producers in my part of the country. His own department now projects net farm income in Saskatchewan for this year at less than $5,000 per farm-$5,000 per farm. It is the lowest since the annus horribilus of 1938.
Will the minister tell us today about the timing and amount of his third line of defence deficiency payment? Will he be making that announcement before seeding begins very shortly?

Mr. Speaker, most of us who follow this issue do not need to go to a committee to find out there is difficulty in the Saskatchewan farm economy. Some of us have been there for a long time and know some of the difficulties.
With regard to what we intend to do, let me say again, there is a considerable amount of money on the table put there by both the federal and provincial governments and the producers. The tone and the substance that I heard this morning of some of the things that were suggested are dead on. We have to work together to solve the problem. We need more education and training and we need better long-term planning. Nobody was in favour of ad hoc programs. That is the approach we intend to pursue.

Mr. Speaker, if I am correct, the minister was not present for the brief given by the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool which is the largest farm organization in Saskatchewan and has been around the longest.
Is the minister assured that the tripartite stabilization program is compatible with the Dunkel income base proposals at the GATT? If not, will he indicate to the House today that he will implement an income base program this calendar year?

Mr. Speaker, just to correct him on the nuance, the longest serving farm organization we heard this morning was the Saskatchewan Association of Rural Municipalities. It came into being when Saskatchewan was formed in 1905.
I say again that we intend to pursue the course we are presently pursuing. That is to work with farmers and
Oral Questions
organizations together to develop the best possible farm program to support farmers in this time of need.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the minister.
The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool has estimated that the net farm income in that province will have a shortfall this year of $1 billion. That slashes in two the net farm income of 1992 which spawned the rally of 13,000 farmers in Saskatoon in January.
The minister is talking about co-operation. What the farmers need is cash. Is the minister going to bring forth an emergency assistance program before spring seeding this year?

Mr. Speaker, I say again that we intend to do what we have been doing. That is to work with the amount of money that is presently on the table, that is contributed by both levels of government and by the producers, to see if we can design a program that will be of maximum assistance to producers. That is exactly what we intend to do.

Mr. Speaker, the major farm organizations from Saskatchewan that made presentations today outlined the deficiency of the Gross Revenue Insurance Program, the government's major stabilization program. They outlined how net farm income is going to drop from over $650 million to some $238 million this year. They outlined clearly that this program is deficient.
Is the minister prepared to make major changes to this program so that these people can stay on their land and so that they can survive at this time when major trade wars are causing this tremendous slump in net farm income? Is he prepared to bring in changes to that program so that it will be adequate?

Mr. Speaker, we have said all along that we are prepared to consider any kind of changes. I do not know what he means by major changes. We would have to make a judgment on that, but certainly we are prepared to make changes and some pretty significant ones if everybody could agree on the changes and everybody could agree that they were going to be in the best interests of the people we are trying to serve.

March 30, 1993
Oral Questions
If the hon. member has some specific ideas, we would be more than happy to hear from him. It is very easy for people to stand up and say that they find the GRIP program flawed and it has major deficiencies in it, but I have yet to have somebody come forward and tell me how they could improve it working with the same amount of money that we presently put into the GRIP program.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister for International Trade.
This government has never fulfilled its promise to bring forward legislation that would ban large-scale Canadian water exports. Protection of Canadian water is a major concern to Canadians, particularly in my province of B.C.
Will the minister give an unequivocal answer today? Is this government prepared to introduce legislation that will prohibit outright large-scale freshwater exports and strictly regulate small-scale water sales such as those by tanker?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought we had dealt with that question through her colleague, the member for Kamloops. He asked the question on a number of occasions. I gave him some very clear answers which basically said that the large scale exports of water are not covered under the NAFTA. They are simply not covered under the NAFTA and that is made absolutely clear by the legislation that is before the House now.
My hon. friend is suggesting that we should go and negotiate something that no one else wants to negotiate. If that is what my hon. friend wants to do then I would say to her that she is trying to give away something that needs not to be given away.

Mr. Speaker, the minister's confusion on this issue is distressing to all of us.
It is a fact that water is a tradable commodity under the free trade agreement with the U.S. and in the
proposed deal with Mexico. His government refused to introduce domestic legislation to prevent water exports, yet the Conservatives have signed two trade agreements that will allow large scale water exports.
Will the minister finally come clean with Canadians and admit it is Tory policy to export Canadian water to the U.S.?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker let me quote if I might from the free trade agreement: "For greater certainty nothing in this act or the agreement except article 302 of the agreement applies to water. In this section water means natural surface and ground water in liquid, gaseous, or solid state, but does not include water packaged as a beverage or in tanks".
In other words, the only water that is covered in the free trade agreement is water that is in a bottle, water that is in a glass, water that is in a truck and water that people want to drink on the other side of the border that is not going in any other way except in a container like a bottle, a glass or a truck.

Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my friend the minister of fisheries. It has to do with his proposed fisheries reforms. His plan to create one board for the Atlantic fishery pits one province against the other, pits one sector against the other. What is even worse, the board is going to be accountable to absolutely no one.
I want to know what the minister is up to. Is he simply trying to insulate himself from criticism for fishery decisions? Why the mad rush to wash his hands of responsibility for the fishing industry?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it certainly has taken some time for the hon. gentleman to catch on to what is up because this started with a discussion paper issued in November 1991. We are obviously not trying to railroad anything through either the House or the governmental system.
What is proposed is a board to undertake some of the responsibilities of the minister of fisheries of Canada
March 30, 1993

with respect to issuing licences to allocations and as an enforcement agency so that we can better enforce the rules in the fishery. Rather than proceeding through the courts, enforcement will be done with respect to conditions that are violated by fishermen if they violate such conditions including conservation decisions.
The policy will still be made by the minister of fisheries and the department, but the board will undertake certain activities which up to now have been done by the minister who has complete and arbitrary power over these matters and who no longer wants it. He wants to be accountable and open to the public.

Mr. Speaker, the minister knows full well despite what he just asserted that this board is not going to be accountable and open to the public. It is going to be accountable and open to no one.
The first thing this board needs if it is going to be useful is some kind of a process for redress. It would also need to be structured along provincial lines where the various fisheries are very different from one province to the other.
On this one would the minister swallow his pride of authorship, go back to the drawing-board, back off this demented twisted scheme and come up with an arrangement that better reflects the concerns of each of the Atlantic provinces and Quebec and the concerns of the fishing industry itself?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been extensive consultations with provincial governments, all of whom support this with the exception of one, the Government of Newfoundland, the Edgar Bergen for whom Charlie McCarthy is now speaking. That is the only government opposing this on entirely fallacious grounds. Otherwise the industry generally is supportive of this. We have had a dialogue with them.
I just met with the industry of the Atlantic coast an hour ago. I met with the B.C. industry last week. Believe me, they all think this is a step forward, with the exception of Uncle Charlie Wells down in St. John's who is opposed to it. He wants something he calls joint management which has nothing to do with this topic at all, but which he hopes to use as an election ploy.
Oral Questions
I am sure the hon. gentleman would not encourage him in that.

Mr. Speaker, my question is also for the minister of fisheries.
This past weekend I met with the chairmen of 14 fisheries committees on the Baie Verte peninsula. The chairmen of those fisheries committees on the Baie Verte peninsula unanimously asked me to convey to the minister of fisheries that they reject this proposal for a management board. They are not interested in elections and they are not interested in ploys.
In no other resource sector, be it forestry, be it mining, be it agriculture, does the minister responsible turn over his responsibilities to a board that is not accountable to anybody.
I want to ask this minister whether he believes that the capacity of fishermen affected by the northern cod moratorium to get justice this past year would have been fully utilized had there been a board rather than a minister who was answerable to fishermen to put in place a proper compensation program.

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if the hon. gentleman received these suggestions from the fishermen that he says he received, then obviously they did not understand and he did not enlighten them as to what the true purpose of this board is.
This board is simply to undertake questions of licensing for example. Should the minister of fisheries be deciding on his own whether John Brown or John Smith should get a licence and not have to give any reasons for that? It would be much better to have a quasi-judicial board which will be able to see to these processes. After having hearings it will give its decisions in writing where everything will be on the public record, rather than some hoary old minister of fisheries, h-o-a-r-y by the way, making these decisions.

Mr. Speaker, the minister of fisheries may think this is a laughing matter, but we are talking about a resource that is absolutely crucial to the economy of the province, in this case Newfoundland and Labrador, and the other Atlantic provinces as well.

March 30, 1993
Oral Questions
The proposed new licensing policy of this minister would have the effect of eliminating from the fishery the fishermen who participated on the basis of a family partnership and have been in the industry for 25 or 30 years because of technical details. As it now stands those fishermen can appeal their being caught up in that web of bureaucratic red tape but under a new board they would be lost.
Does the minister recognize that fishermen, just like people in the agricultural industry, people in the forestry industry, people in the mining industry want to retain the ability to appeal directly to their elected representatives and to their government and not to some unaccountable board about their very livelihood?
Will the minister put aside this foolish and cowardly idea?

speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister of Fisheries and Oceans and Minister for the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Fisheries and Oceans
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentleman is confusing two matters. With respect to licensing there are going to be major changes made for the future. In the groundfish fishery we will license professional fulltime fishermen who have a permanent attachment to the fishery. We can no longer afford the luxury of allowing anyone to go throw their nets in the water and fish. They will have to be certified and professional.
At the present time to whom do they appeal if they are turned down in a licensing application? To the minister. Does he have to give any reasons for his decision? No, he does not. To whom will they appeal in the future? To a quasi-judicial independent board which will have to give written reasons for its decision. I suggest they will be much better off out of the political circus and before quasi-judicial process than they are today.
Might I just say that we had Charlie McCarthy in the Elouse and now we have Mortimer Snerd on the other side.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister for International Trade.
While Investment Canada has been made a virtual toothless tiger in protecting Canadian high technology industry, the Americans have protected theirs well.
I want to ask the Minister for International Trade whether he would confirm that under provisions of the United States' trade law which are not subject to NAFTA or the FTA or to any challenge or any dispute settlement processes, the United States can block virtually any Canadian investment in the U.S. high technology industry by invoking even the slightest relationship to national security?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think my hon. friend is grossly exaggerating the point in the question he has just asked.
There is a provision under U.S. law which is used very sparingly that relates to acquisitions which could be characterized as affecting national security. My understanding is that it has been used in a handful of situations.

Mr. Speaker, I guess the Minister for International Trade has never heard of Sematech which is the United States' semiconductor consortium that controls 35 per cent of the international market. It is supported by the Pentagon and therefore excludes Canadian investment.
Maybe he has heard of the American high resolution television industry also supported by the Pentagon from which Canadian participation is excluded.

Television. Is it not clear to the minister that what we have is a very asymmetric deal? Canadian high technology can be bought left and right. The Americans just invoke national security which is everything and we are out of the game.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has used two examples. I think that counts as something like less than a handful.
If my hon. friend looks at the balance in the free trade agreement he will see there is a considerable degree of protection for large Canadian companies with assets over $150 million that the United States does not have.
March 30, 1993

We have that element of protection through Investment Canada. The United States does not have that.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Finance.
One way my community and other communities are trying to stimulate economic activity is by helping local people start their own businesses through entrepreneurship programs and training programs. However when these individuals go to banks and traditional institutions they are told that they do not fit within the traditional lending formula. The Small Businesses Loans Act will help, as will other measures.
I would ask the minister if he will consider this difficulty in his upcoming budget and take some steps to help communities such as mine establish community equity funds or venture capital funds which can be used to help finance existing businesses or new businesses that are innovative and can help our local economy?

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his question. I particularly thank him for making reference to the changes that have been introduced to the Small Businesses Loans Act for which I thank all hon. members. I think everyone will agree that it is a vast improvement.
In so far as his question about community venture capital funds is concerned, I will take that as a representation. I should remind him that we have made changes to the way we treat RRSPs and also the activities related to the labour sponsored venture capital corporations which I believe has gone a long way in helping the important small business sector in providing capital for investment.
I appreciate the hon. member's interest and I assure him I will take his representation seriously.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the
Oral Questions
Minister of Finance. As the minister knows labour unions in this country collect tax subsidized dues and earn tax-free income on their investments.
In 1990 Canadian and international unions collected $796 million in tax deductible dues. The cost in lost tax revenues to the federal and provincial governments could exceed $300 million a year. These same unions enjoyed $52 million in revenue on their invested assets all tax free.
Does the minister agree that the unions' tax status should be reviewed so that the tax system will be fairer and more equitable for all Canadians? Surely this tax loophole should be closed.

speakeroldname: Hon. Don Mazankowski (Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Deputy Prime Minister; Minister of Finance; Vice-President
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, union dues are deductible for much the same reasons as other professional membership fees.
The tax exempt status of unions is treated in much the same way as Canadian non-profit organizations. I appreciate however the hon. member bringing this to my attention.
I have noted the article in the newspaper outlining the very point which the hon. member raises in the House today. I will certainly examine it and get back to the hon. member.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday in the House I tried to ask a question of the minister of health. He was away and I would like to try again today.
The suicide rate in the Nishnawbe-Aski Nation territory continues to be alarming to the rest of us. In the last year alone there have been over a dozen suicides in the Nishnawbe-Aski Nation.
From the beginning of this year until now there have already been seven suicides in the Nishnawbe-Aski Nation. The minister has received a proposal from the Nishnawbe-Aski Nation to put in place an inquiry into the suicide crisis in northern Ontario.

March 30, 1993
Oral Questions
I would like to ask the minister who is in the House today whether he could tell us if he is prepared at this time to look at this kind of inquiry into this very desperate situation in northern Ontario?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe that all members of the House share the member's concern about the Nish-nawbe-Aski Nation's problem of suicide.
The proposal made by Chief Morris, who I met with last week, talks about an inquiry with a format that would include disclosures by young people and would provide a safety net for these young people to assist them to cope with the potential effects of public disclosures.
It is a very delicate operation. We understand that when we ask young people to expose the problems they face, such as sexual abuse or that kind of issue, it can make it very difficult for them.
This morning I had a long discussion with the officials of the department. I decided that with the collaboration of the Government of Ontario and the nation itself I would be ready to move ahead with an inquiry if I had the guarantees that a few conditions are respected, that the young people involved will be assisted and it will be done in light of the consequences they face.
If it is fact that once again it will be the Government of Ontario and the nation itself I would be ready to say yes to the proposal.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the minister for his answer.
I would like to ask a very important question which relates to the inquiry and the effect it may have on the present crisis that we face.
It is well known that an inquiry could take up to 18 months. During this process it is incumbent upon the House and the department of health to understand that there are programs available now that we can put in place, if the resources are available, so that the crisis we are dealing with will not be delayed for 18 months as the inquiry is going on.
Would the minister be prepared to continue to fund and look at individual proposals from communities for crisis intervention programs so that we can continue with the work that we started last week at the suicide prevention workshop in order that the situation we are dealing with, the crisis of the suicides, will not go unresolved until the inquiry is over?

speakeroldname: Hon. Benoit Bouchard (Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, obviously the work being done will continue to be done.
I would like to correct something that Chief Morris said last week. He said that we have not done anything to alleviate the problems in the communities. For 1992-93, we have provided $1,400,000 to help the communities to deal with the problems and we will continue to do that.
As I said to Chief Morris last week, he should recognize the work done by the Government of Canada to help the community to deal with the suicide problem.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the government House leader.
Yesterday the minister stated that the reason for not releasing 25 pages of censored documents was because of the Privacy Act. We now know that that is not true.
Second, the minister said that the Government of Canada was co-operating 100 per cent with the commission of inquiry in Nova Scotia.
Earlier today the chief legal counsel of the Westray mine public inquiry said: "The federal government has not released all of its Westray mine documents to the inquiry".
Why has the government House leader and other members of the federal cabinet continually told members of the House that all of the documentation and co-operation was forthcoming from the Government of Canada to the commission of inquiry in Nova Scotia when in fact it was not?

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister for Science and Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)):
speakerposition: Minister for Science; Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
speechtext:
