Mr. Speaker, I was saying prior to the break at lunch time that this particular statute change is one which will remove the right to all of the $100,000 exemption with respect to speculative real estate or with respect to non-producing real estate.
This is a budgetary measure. The effect of the $100,000 allowance applied to real estate that is a static investment reduces the revenue of the government very considerably. Over a five-year period the result of the tax change will increase the revenues of the government by $980 million a year, and will probably slightly increase every year from then on.
It is difficult to determine how much it is really going to work out to because it is a tax on the increase in sale value of real estate. If real estate prices do not advance then perhaps it will not be as much. If real estate prices advance more then the gain may be even more.
The concept here is to take away a break in the tax system that was designed to encourage effective job producing investment and make sure that investment break is only toward effective job producing investment. In other words, at the present time this benefit can be used for any piece of real estate a person might hold, and dead real estate, even if it is rental real estate, is not an effective job producing investment.
In terms of rental real estate, the Income Tax Act is still very favourable. Rental real estate is able to take a capital cost allowance and deduct that against rents received. The same applies with respect to the deduction of mortgage interest applicable to the investment so that there is a profit in holding rental real estate. The fact is that rental real estate is not a job producing investment and therefore it is felt by the government that in future that type of investment should not receive the $100,000 advantage.
The proposal by the government being contested in this suggested amendment by the member for Sudbury is that this restriction on the use of the $100,000 be eliminated. This is an important restriction. It is a very
March 30,1993

necessary restriction in terms of income to the government from the tax system and it is inappropriate for the House at this point, certainly in view of the fiscal status of the country, to expect that this benefit continue.
Those who presently have static real estate can continue to claim the $100,000 deduction against their existing real estate holdings but they can only claim it as a proportion of the period of time they have held the investment. For example, if they have held a piece of static real estate from 1972 forward, this year being 1993, they would be able to have a 21 fraction of the $100,000 tax-free gain.
As years go by the percentage of tax-free gain goes down, but nonetheless they will still be able to have a very substantial tax-free advantage applicable to the gain on non-producing property.
With respect to producing real estate, which is real estate property held as part of a business, if one owns a store and is running a hardware store from it then that is real estate that is part of the business. That can be sold as part of the business and the $100,000 applies. In the case of a small business the $500,000 allowance would apply on its shares. We are not affecting businesses as businesses. We are affecting static real estate investment.
I am indeed surprised that members opposite would want to make sure that benefit is still in the Income Tax Act. I think on reflection they may agree with the government that the $100,000 allowance is not proper in this particular case and ought not to be allowed and that the government's change in the statute ought to proceed as the bill indicates.

The carpenters, electricians, plumbers, gardeners and all of the people who are in the renovation business in my city of Toronto are being hurt by this particular amendment to the tax act. It has effectively shut down the incentive for people to get involved with that second home, that second piece of property.
The member for Mississauga South comes from the same community, although he is from Mississauga where there are a lot of large, brand new homes and there probably would not be as much renovation. However, in the downtown areas where there are constant renovations and renewals there is a whole new industry developing where people are working in a craftsman-like way, renewing and renovating these homes. A lot of that industry comes from individuals who take on a second property as an investment.
I do not think the government has in fact really done an analysis as to whether or not this is effectively producing jobs. It is a funny thing with this government. It has managed to put forward the image that it is a great fiscal manager with its lean, mean machine approach to our deficit and our debt. This is where the Liberal Party is totally different from the Conservative Party. When we go through a global recession just like the one we have been through and the one in 1981-82, we made sure we had programs because we believed that it was more important to take people off welfare and the unemployment insurance rolls and put them back to work. This particular motion is another example of where the bean counters over there in finance have said: "Oh, if we disallow this exemption in the interest of fiscal responsibility, then we are much further ahead". Mr. Speaker, those who thought I was much older than 50 are amazed when they hear such kind words.

The lifetime capital gains exemption was introduced in order to encourage investment, risk taking and broader individual participation in equity markets. These are all goals to which the government is as committed today as it was when the exemption was first introduced in 1985.
However, as with any legislation, it is necessary to continually assess the effectiveness with which the exemption meets these objectives and to weigh these objectives against the need for fiscal responsibility.
In keeping with this, the government is proposing-effective for 1992 and subsequent taxation years-to amend the rules governing the availability of the lifetime capital gains exemption.
Specifically the exemption will no longer be available in respect of most gains of an individual on the sale of real estate purchased after February 1992 that is not used in an active business carried on by the individual.
March 30, 1993

Individuals who purchased real estate before this date will, however, still be eligible to benefit from exemption in respect of a pro rata portion of any gain that they realize.
The portion of the gain that will continue to be eligible for the exemption will be determined on the basis of a formula that notionally allocates any gain over the ownership period. That portion of the gain that is allocated to the period prior to March 1992 will qualify for the exemption.
Thus, if an individual realized a $15,000 capital gain on land that was purchased in March 1990 and sold in February 1993, two-thirds of the gain or $10,000 will be eligible for the exemption.
These changes are in no way a reversal of the government's original intention in introducing the lifetime capital gains exemption. Rather, they are intended to help direct resources toward those investments such as equities that will best enhance Canada's ability to compete in international markets.
In this manner they respond to the economy's growing need for investment funds and will ensure that the lifetime capital gains exemption will continue to represent a major incentive for Canadians to invest.
Finally, it is not clear that these changes will have an adverse impact on the provision of private rental accommodation. It is clear that speculative real estate ventures will be less attractive thereby easing the upward pressure on real estate prices. This, in turn, could potentially increase the yields on investments that may be realized through rent as opposed to capital gains on real property.
I would like to recap what I said earlier today just a few minutes ago and make some comments on four major objectives.
First, the objective of the capital gains exemption is to encourage risk taking and broader and individual participation in equity markets.
Second, it is necessary to assess the effectiveness with which the exemption meets these objectives and to weigh these objectives against the need for fiscal responsibility.

Third, by restricting the availability of the exemption, the government is responding to the economy's growing need for investment funds. This will help direct resources to those investments that will best enhance Canada's international competitiveness.

Now here we are back in the House. The clause has been reintroduced absolutely word for word in its original form. It is a despicable way of behaving for people who are going around the country saying they wish to have a reform of the parliamentary institutions. What kind of reform is it going to want when the only thing it understands is that if it makes a decision, it has to be its way and that is it. The government reintroduced this clause with absolutely no changes, without answering the questions and the fears of employees. This is a serious matter. The government should withdraw the motion which reintroduces this clause in order to facilitate and
to open up the debate and to make it a more honest approach.
I would ask the government to at least defend its position. Members should explain to the people of Canada, to their employees, why it has reintroduced this clause in word for word fashion without answering the fears of its employees.
Nobody else will have the same kind of rules apply to them. Imagine, Mr. Speaker, if your tax return information could be accessed by your boss to be used in some way against you if it is thought that you are not performing your job properly. No one else has that privilege.
If an employee does anything with his own personal tax return which is not right, he should be subjected to exactly the same rules as all other Canadians. In effect, this clause will remove that.
It is a serious matter. Perhaps there are reasons for doing this. It certainly was not clear at committee and there was not a lot of discussion on it. I would ask that this motion be withdrawn.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel R. Tremblay (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, you know how much I respect the hon. member for Sudbury. I did not want to precede her; I just wanted to offer her the floor before me on report stage of Bill C-92.
The amendment in question would put back in Bill C-92 the clause deleted by the finance committee. This clause, former clause 137, amends some rules on the confidentiality of information in section 241 of the Income Thx Act. Section 241 forbids officials to use or communicate information obtained under the act unless expressly authorized in one of the exemptions provided in that section.
I think that the former clause 137 should be restored for three reasons.
First, in addition to the amendment considered by the finance committee, this clause makes some improvements to section 241 of the act. For example, one of the improvements is that rules on the confidentiality of information do not apply to information that does not directly or indirectly identify the taxpayer.
March 30, 1993

This would confirm Revenue Canada's ability to publish summary data or statistics needed to develop social and fiscal policy. These data are also very widely used by the business community.
Another important amendment would allow Revenue Canada to use a taxpayer's address to send him information. Thus Revenue Canada could provide a service like the mail service available through the American tax authorities in medical or legal emergencies.
Another amendment says that confidential information can be provided to provincial governments for evaluating or formulating tax policy. This amendment would also allow providing confidential information to provincial officials responsible for applying or enforcing a federal tax law. That is important, for example, when the Quebec Department of Revenue collects the GST for the federal government.
The second reason for reinstating former clause 137 is that without this clause certain amendments to another clause in the bill would no longer serve any purpose. More specifically, clause 136 introduces a number of amendments to section 239 of the Income Tax Act which arise from amendments made under former clause 137. Unless the clause is reinstated some of the amendments provided under clause 136 will not make sense. In fact, the relevant provision of section 239 of the act provides that contravening the confidentiality of information rules described under section 241 of the act constitutes an offence. If former clause 137 is not reinstated it would be impossible to enforce this provision in some cases, which could seriously undermine the application of the rules on the confidentiality of information.
These references to certain clauses may be confusing to some, but all members who sat on the finance committee know very well what we are talking about right now.
The third reason for reinstating former clause 137 is that most of the concerns about this clause, based on the right to privacy, have been laid to rest. These concerns arose from the amendment that would allow the use of confidential information for the purposes of surveillance
Government Orders
or evaluation of Revenue Canada employees or of disciplinary measures imposed on these employees.
I would like to explain briefly why it was necessary to introduce this amendment.
Until recently senior management at Revenue Canada, Taxation, considered that the department's mandate for applying tax legislation allowed it to use confidential information for the purpose of supervising and evaluating its employees and taking disciplinary action in their regard. For instance, if a Revenue Canada employee used information concerning another taxpayer for his own purposes or if the employee falsified information in his own tax return in order to take advantage of insider information on the department's assessment and audit practices, Revenue Canada managers assumed they could use that information to take appropriate disciplinary action.
However, in 1987 the Federal Court maintained that this particular use of information by management contravened the rules on the confidentiality of information. Consequently it is impossible to submit confidential information to support the disciplinary action proposed in a particular case. The fact remains that relevant confidential information can always be submitted as evidence when charges are laid, as is sometimes the case. However, in other less serious situations it is more appropriate to take disciplinary action than to lay charges, and even in cases where charges are laid Revenue Canada managers must be able to take temporary disciplinary action, pending the outcome of the case, in order to safeguard the integrity of the tax system.
The proposed amendments would allow the use of confidential information in the case of disciplinary proceedings, as was the case before the decision handed down by the Federal Court in 1987. This particular use would however be qualified by new safety measures to make sure that only relevant confidential information is used and to prevent disclosure of information submitted before a disciplinary tribunal. The person chairing the proceedings would be authorized to order a hearing to be held in camera and to impose a ban on publication of the information or measures in question in order to protect the identity of the taxpayer.

March 30, 1993
Government Orders
Many of the concerns about this amendment were raised by privacy commissioner, Bruce Phillips, who was afraid that the amendment would impinge on the right to privacy of Revenue Canada employees and that it would give departmental managers undue authority over their employees. However these fears were allayed after discussions and exchanges of letters between Mr. Phillips and national revenue deputy minister Pierre Gra-velle.
To prove my point I would like to read a few paragraphs from a letter written by Mr. Phillips, which the deputy minister of national revenue was kind enough to give me. The finance committee did not have the opportunity to see this letter before voting on Bill C-92. The letter is dated March 23, 1993 and it is addressed to Mr. Gravelle. With your permission, I will read some excerpts of this letter, which I was kindly given. I am making an ad hoc translation.
Thank you for your letter of March 23, 1993 on the proposed amendments to the Income Thx Act and the Excise Tix Act, as well as the concerns which I raised in my letter of March 18.
I first want to tell you how pleased I was with the tone and the substance of your letter. Indeed, you readily recognize the importance of issues related to privacy and you propose to hold consultations to develop safeguards for protecting the right to privacy when disciplinary action is taken.
You mention that I did not disagree that you have the right, indeed the obligation, to ensure the total honesty of your employees, and particularly to make sure that no employee uses insider information for his or her personal benefit. I am convinced that all Canadians support this objective.
My concern has to do with potential abuse, and I proposed, as a possible approach, setting strict criteria for the disciplinary review of employee files, such as defining what constitutes reasonable grounds.
I am therefore pleased to see that you have undertaken to develop guidelines on this issue and that you are willing to discuss them with people from my office and others concerned. I am very pleased with this proposal and I am confident that together we can come up with a satisfactory solution which will protect the employees' right to privacy.
As I said earlier, this is an excerpt from a letter dealing with Bill C-92, which was addressed to Mr. Gravelle, the deputy minister-

Mr. Speaker, the hon. member speaking just quoted excerpts from a letter. He repeated it three times. I heard him say that he had the full letter in his hand. According to the rules of procedure the member must, if called upon, table the complete letter forthwith. I ask Mr. Speaker to make that ruling.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have before me the whole letter from Bruce Phillips to Pierre Gravelle, dated March 23, to which I was referring. This letter is in English and I translated it as I went along. My comments apply to the whole letter. I will be pleased to include with my notes the full text of the letter, which is a public document in any case.
With your permission, I will now carry on.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I first want to remind the hon. members of the usual practice in the House. A member can ask for the tabling of a document by a minister, however, in the case of a member, even though he or she may be a parliamentary secretary, it is up to that person to comply. I understand that the hon. member has no objection to tabling that document.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that the minister will object to the tabling of a letter which is already a public document.
The Privacy Commissioner of Canada is convinced, as I am, that by holding consultations with his office and with others concerned, such as the Public Service Alliance of Canada and other unions representing Revenue Canada employees, this department will be able to develop guidelines for protecting the legitimate privacy interests of its employees.
I maintain that these guidelines, along with the legislative proposals included in the former clause 137, will ensure a fair balance between the different interests involved.
Since my time is running out quickly, I recommend that the House adopt the motion to amend Bill C-92 by reinstating the former clause 137.
March 30, 1993

Mr. Speaker, the letter that the hon. member was quoting from was a letter in response to Mr. Phillips from the deputy minister. The member stands up in the House and says:"Oh, I have a copy of a letter here from Mr. Bruce Phillips who is the privacy commissioner to the deputy minister". He quotes from one letter and then claims he has the other letter in his hand. I do not want the other letter. That was in the news media. I want the letter that he was quoting from. I would maintain that a parliamentary secretary has the same status in this Chamber as a minister.
It is important to see what has happened here. What has happened in this House is this. Let me just take us back a week. There was a national news story across Canada. The national news story said that the privacy commissioner had concerns about what was in this bill. The committee voted to take out the clause relating to the so-called invasion of privacy. The clause says that certain people can have their income tax returns examined. There have been no criminal charges laid because of course once you do that you can get it examined anyway. This allows a specific employer to take somebody's personal income tax return, namely an employee of the Government of Canada working at Revenue Canada, and it allows the boss to look at his income tax return to discipline him. That is why the committee took it out.
It made the news right across Canada. The committee decided to take out that clause. Then the committee, having seen a victory, shortened its hearings because no witnesses were called. The privacy commissioner was off the hook and the bill went through the committee. Now we are back in the House of Commons and they are reintroducing the clause they took out in the committee to shorten the committee hearings.
What would you call that? It is an interesting study in parliamentary procedure. I am sure that the clerks at the table and people who write in such magazines as The Parliamentarian and political science students will be able to do a masters thesis on this one. This is a precedent I would say in the British tradition of parliamentary procedure to have a clause taken out in a committee. The committee then reports back the bill, satisfied that it has done its job. There were no hearings on that clause at all, no hearings from the privacy commissioner who
Government Orders
said: "You are violating the rights of people in Canada to have their income tax returns taken and looked at by your boss to discipline you".
It was taken out and the bill passes because the clause is out. It comes before the House with a majority vote in the House of Commons to reintroduce the clause during closure and have it passed. The privacy commissioner, Bruce Phillips, was absolutely correct in his judgment. The government is doing something against what the privacy commission made a big fuss about in the media last week. There is such a thing on the back of every income tax return called the "Declaration of Taxpayer Rights".
You will see it on the back of every single booklet for income tax purposes. It says: "Declaration of Taxpayer Rights". It has been there, my goodness, ever since I can recall. It is a declaration of taxpayer rights in dealings with Revenue Canada, Taxation. You have important rights.
In a section of the declaration of taxpayer rights, it reads: "Privacy and confidentiality". Let me just read the sentence. It says: "You are entitled to expect that we will use the personal and financial information you provide us only for purposes the law allows". The law allows.
This is the law that we are passing today. This is the amendment that we are sticking into that law that we are passing today. That will be the law of Canada. It will be that which the law allows. What will the law allow?
It will allow an employee of Revenue Canada to have his or her personal income tax return taken out to be examined for "surveillance purposes" for "disciplinary actions" without laying charges. As the law presently stands if you do not lay the charges you do not get to look at the income tax return.
This will allow them to do it without any other reason except the boss having an inkling or a feeling. If he does not like the looks of a person, if he does not like the way a person is acting in Revenue Canada, all those employees now can have their personal income tax returns looked at and examined.
We have a division of Revenue Canada called the audit branch. There are 14.6 million returns filed in Canada. There are 35,000 returns on average that are re-examined. They are audited. If you work it out that works out to one chance in 430 years of having your income tax

March 30,1993
Government Orders
return examined in a manner that we are prescribing under this new clause.
In other words, for you to be audited it is once every 430 years if the law is not discriminating against you if you are an ordinary Canadian. If you have done something wrong in your income tax return of course you can be liable. If some little thing is wrong there are fines of up to $25,000 and jail for one year.
Now we will have a new class of people in Canada whose income tax returns can be taken out at any time. They can be judgeu as to whether or not they can get a promotion. Their personal finances are looked at, who they are paying money to and which educational institution they support. What are their deductions? What are their personal and financial circumstances? What are people doing in their families? Exactly what is the condition of each person in that family? What are they doing? Everything.
We are passing this on an excuse. The minister says: "For possible disciplinary actions without laying charges", "for surveillance of employees at Revenue Canada", "to allow supervisors to obtain the private information of somebody's income tax return", "to allow the government to give surveillance to employees of Revenue Canada".
Can you imagine what the employees of Revenue Canada are feeling today having this special law just for them?
They will now be under a microscope because the Parliament of Canada has decided to defy what the privacy commissioner said last week publicly in the newspapers in this country. Members of Parliament decided when they went into their standing committee that somebody behind the scenes was going to pull a fast one and they were going to get the thing out of the public view by withdrawing the clause. All the government members sat there and refused to vote.
If I am wrong on this let me be corrected now. They supported it by their silence because they knew that it was going to be brought back in a sneaky fashion and reintroduced through the strict majority of this Chamber.
This is an outrage. We should have a hearing by the privacy commissioner before the House of Commons.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order. Have we totally abandoned the way we normally do business here? We have had a government member and two Liberal members. It is about time we had an NDP spokesperson on this.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I have no problem giving the floor, but in the tradition of this House the Speaker watches the two sides of the House. After this side, I have my eyes on the other side. It is the tradition. If the hon. member wants to speak absolutely, I have no problem.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps inadvertently I changed what might have been your normal procedure because I was simply getting up, not because I had been planning to, but because I wanted to respond to what the hon. member who just spoke stated. I wanted to do that in a timely fashion. I was completely prepared to allow the hon. member from Winnipeg to go ahead if he wishes. Perhaps I could just intervene here on this point.
The member has just talked about a process which included a committee of which I was the chairman. I think perhaps I could elucidate slightly about the procedure that was followed because perhaps inadvertently he has heard about the procedure. As I recall he was not there so he must have read or heard about it or otherwise got his information.
We are dealing here with a bill with probably 200 to 250 pages that incorporates many different changes to the Income Thx Act, what we often call a technical bill. Basically it is a bill which is picking up all kinds of different things which have accumulated over the course of a year and putting them into a bill.
One of those things happens to do with the matter that the hon. member is speaking about in the question of the utilization of tax returns of Revenue Canada employees in the evaluation of their work or in cases which may involve them in terms of their own personal tax liability.
What happened in committee was that this matter was brought to our attention very late in the committee process. The bill had been referred to committee. We had examined the matters that had been raised and of interest and in particular the one spoke of here earlier today about trusts where we invited some people to come and talk about that.
March 30, 1993

This matter only came to our attention at a point in time when we were doing clause by clause. Given the fact that this matter was not necessary in terms of the remainder of the bill, at the time the thought was that we could proceed with the remainder of the bill and allow this matter if you like to be defeated or to stand aside because it did not have anything to do with the integrity of the rest of the bill. We were in fact conceding this matter in order to pass 99 per cent of the bill.
What happened is that the union representing Revenue Canada employees had raised the matter. It raised it with the privacy commissioner as well. He wrote a letter to me advising of his concern. We were going to deal with that. We were interrupted that day because of a vote in this House. We discovered after that that in fact there had been subsequent action. The deputy minister of Revenue Canada had responded to the letter of the privacy commissioner and subsequently the privacy commissioner responded to the deputy minister for Revenue Canada saying that he was satisfied with the response and the process and that his concerns had been alleviated. All those letters are a matter of public record and if anybody wishes to have them I can make them available because I have them. I have circulated them to all members of the finance committee. I believe members of his own party should have them, but if not I can make them available. Those letters outline the exchange.
The understanding of many members, including myself, was that over the course of time between the passing of the bill and its returning to the House, members would have an opportunity to examine the issue, see the exchange of correspondence that had taken place and then come to a proper conclusion.
Whether the idea of incorporating or allowing the tax returns of employees of Revenue Canada to be used in cases where they were involved to be entered into evidence is a matter on which members can come to their conclusion. However I just want to speak to the process.
The process was not that members in some way defeated this. The expectation at the time was that members would apprise themselves of the exchange of correspondence and any other facts that they might not
Government Orders
be aware of at that time. It was a way to let the bill proceed expeditiously.
On the question of whether this information should be allowed to be used for the purposes of Revenue Canada in its administration of the Income Thx Act, this was the practice at Revenue Canada for many years. It was a court decision a couple of years ago. The Revenue Canada Act states that this information can only be used for the purposes of the act. Revenue Canada had always interpreted that to mean that administering the Revenue Canada Act included administering its own employees and on that basis could use this information. The courts defined more narrowly.
This measure seeks to suggest that where a Revenue Canada employee may have been involved in a matter that may have involved a taxpayer and there may have been a fraud, a breach of trust or some other matter, that the income tax return of that employee could be relevant to the particular case and could be used in evidence before a tribunal that involved this employee.
Again it is up to members to debate the merits of that, but that is what this matter seeks to do. It re-establishes a practice that had been there in the past. The process used was to expedite the passage of the bill. There was no objection to most of the other measures.

speechtext: I want to remind the hon. member that this is only a notice. This does not necessarily mean that government will act on this notice. For the time being, it is nothing more than a notice given to this House. Therefore, no motion per se has been put before this House.

The House resumed consideration of Bill C-92, an act to amend the Income Thx Act, the Canada Pension Plan, the Income Thx Conventions Interpretation Act, the Ihx Rebate Discounting Act, the Unemployment Insurance Act and certain related acts, as reported (with amendment) from the Standing Committee on Finance; and Motion No. 4.

Mr. Speaker, the notice given by the minister just previously may be procedurally acceptable, but it is certainly not acceptable in any moral or parliamentary way.
We have only just begun debate on the North American free trade agreement and already the government is moving time allocation. It is certainly something on which I have made representations to the Chair. I hope now that the government's intentions are clear that the Chair will respond to my letter of Thursday last week with some expedience and with favour I hope.
In any event, I appreciated the intervention of the chairman of the finance committee. He has a reputation of being a fair-minded person. I think he gave a reasonable account of things except that it is also fair to say that opposition members have good reason to feel somewhat betrayed by the process.
I know that I as the NDP member on that committee had the impression at one point that when clause 137, which is the motion we are debating now, was defeated it
was for the purposes of either leaving it out altogether or amending it in a way that may have proved acceptable to the opposition or may have proved unacceptable. But I certainly did not expect the government would simply reintroduce it at report stage without any changes at all.
It is perfectly within the government's right to do that but that was not my expectation. Certainly we could have kept things going that evening had we thought that all we were going to be faced with, having done what we did, was the reintroduction of the clause unchanged.
There was some disposition on the part of the government at that time to find an amendment that would meet some of the concerns that were raised by the Public Service Alliance. When the government members said: "Why don't we just defeat the clause and we can deal with this later", I think there was a reasonable expectation on the part of the opposition and of the Public Service Alliance people who were present that there was a willingness to try and deal with it.
The chairman of the committee may argue that it has been dealt with in the sense that the privacy commissioner has dealt with it by saying that the objections which he raised in his conversations and exchange of letters with Mr. Gravelle of Revenue Canada have been dealt with to his satisfaction. However, just because the privacy commissioner is satisfied that there is a willingness to develop safeguards, et cetera, does not mean that the issue simply disappears. The issue did not rely solely on the intervention of the privacy commissioner in the first place. In fact, we did not hear from the privacy commissioner, we heard from the Public Service Alliance of Canada.
It is in that sense that I think the government, even though it is operating within the rules, has not acted in good faith, perhaps not even in a way that the government members on the committee thought it would act. I have no way of knowing exactly what they expected, but my reading at that time was that there was a willingness to try and find some accommodation.
Instead we are faced with the reintroduction of clause 137 exactly as it was. One wonders about the integrity of the committee process in the final analysis. If a committee can defeat a clause only to have the government- the government in the big brother sense of the word-say presumably to the committee members: "That was a fine, independent act you were responsible
March 30, 1993

for in committee but we are sorry, we are going to reintroduce exactly what you permitted to be defeated".
For me, it was one of those times when I really felt that committee work mattered. We got together with the government members and said: "Look, there is a problem here. Let's defeat it". If we had time maybe we could have developed an amendment, but I thought that was forthcoming. There we were working like members of Parliament are supposed to work in the public mind. What happens is the government steps in at some point after and says: "Sorry, we want our way and we want our way exactly the way we want it".
From a kind of political process and parliamentary process point of view, this is an awfully disappointing thing. I am somewhat-I do not know if disappointed is the right word-in the privacy commissioner who in some respects seems to have retreated from his earlier concerns.
Perhaps retreat is a pejorative way to put it. Maybe it is just that he understood things that he did not understand before, whatever the case may be. The fact is that the commitment to develop safeguards is understandably not enough for Revenue Canada employees. For one thing, they do not know what those safeguards will be, whether they will actually be safeguards or whether they will just be phoney guards that safeguard the government in its introduction of this new and much more Draconian measure with respect to access to the tax files of Revenue Canada employees than anything we have ever seen before.
I was certainly persuaded by the testimony we heard and by my own reading of the issue that this is not something the government desperately needs. It has at its disposal other remedies when it feels that an employee of Revenue Canada is somehow using their position in a way that advantages them in terms of their own personal income tax. The government has ways of dealing with that.
I mentioned the court case that the member before me referred to and which officials before the committee referred to frequently in justifying this action. The one thing that they never mentioned was that the person who was the centre of that court case, if I understand things correctly, is not now an employee of Revenue Canada. It is not as if the government was unsuccessful in its
Government Orders
dealing with that person. It did manage to get rid of that person, so to speak.
I think the government is making a serious mistake here. I have a great many Revenue Canada employees in my constituency. I happen to have located in my constituency, Winnipeg Transcona, the taxation data centre for western Canada and I know a great many people who work there. I have walked the picket line with them. I have fought on their behalf, successfully once and unsuccessfully the second time, when the government tried to introduce parking fees and a number of other things.
I find that I share their offence at having the government introduce a measure which puts them in a special category of Canadian taxpayers. I share their offence at being put in this special class of people whose tax files will be available basically at the whim of supervisors or senior management in Revenue Canada.
Maybe this is what the safeguards are intended to deal with, but we will believe that when we see it. When someone is in dispute with management, management will have this extra hammer that they will presumably in an unrelated way, if they so desire, be able to use. TTiey will be able to look into that person's tax files in a totally unprovoked way, that is to say, as far as it pertains to their tax, the way that they are dealing with their taxes, and see if there is not something that they can get on that person, see if there is not something that they can use against that person.
That is a form of discipline and a form of management oversight or intrusion into the privacy of employees that no one else in the country would be expected to tolerate. That is the reason why people who are working for Revenue Canada take offence at this. I think they are justified in taking offence at this. I think that the members of the committee saw the offence that this was to them and to other notions of privacy that we all hold in common.
That is why they defeated it and hoped that it would be dealt with satisfactorily, presumably by an amendment or, failing an amendment that was satisfactory to all the interested parties, by leaving out clause 137 or reintroducing clause 137 without the offending language. I understand that clause 137 contains more than just what

March 30, 1993
Government Orders
we are dealing with here. That was part of a concern expressed by a departmental official who did the very unusual thing of leaping to the table at the committee meeting as if he was a committee member and trying to prevent the committee from doing what it was about to do. Then he was reminded that he was not a member of the committee and that he should take his place as an official.

speakerposition: Assistant Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent to extend the time of the hon. member?
Agreed.

I promise not to go on too long, Mr. Speaker, at the request of my own colleagues.
In any event, there was a way this could have been dealt with so that it could have satisfied the Public Service Alliance of Canada and it could have been an exemplary moment in the life of committees and the relationship between committee and Parliament. Instead, it has turned out to be kind of a dirty deal and one other occasion on which we feel that maybe we were a little bit naive. We should have dragged the committee on and been obstructionist and made absolutely sure that we got exactly what we wanted and done all of those things that we are sometimes condemned for in this place.
This time we did not do that. We said that it looks like there is some goodwill here and there is the possibility for a constructive solution. What happens? We get it in the ear. The clause is reintroduced exactly as it was. That is why we will be voting against it.
It is still the offence that it was in the beginning to the integrity and privacy of Revenue Canada employees. It is beyond that now. It is an offence against the appropriate relationship that ought to obtain with a committee that deletes a clause with the expectation that it will be amended and not reintroduced uncritically at report stage, as it has been.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to make a few comments with respect to what happened in the committee and the reason this amendment is before us.
When we in the committee received the complaint by the Public Service Commission we had already heard all of the witnesses we intended to hear on this bill and were going to go immediately to clause by clause. We decided to break the pattern and call in the Public Service Alliance people to explain their concerns.
We then called Revenue Canada people and unfortunately the bells rang for a vote and we came back.
During the course of that vote period, Bruce Phillips, the privacy commissioner, had re-examined the entire matter and was going to appear as a witness at the committee. Unfortunately it was impossible to carry on the committee in that room much longer and it was necessary for the purpose of moving legislation forward that this bill be passed and this whole issue, which is really a very minor issue in a very large bill, be dealt with at report stage.
Everyone who has been involved in the bill has had a copy of the privacy commissioner's advice concerning the change. Indeed, if people take a look at the matter quite impartially they will note the rationale for the change. The change in the statute is brought about because of a case between the government and a woman by the name of Monica Lau, who is a tax assessor.
Ms. Lau was involved in tax gains in the years 1981, 1982 and 1983. In the course of a disciplinary matter the government used her tax return to fire her because the information on the tax return was essential to show the misfeasance that allowed a person to be fired from the Public Service of Canada.
The complainant took the matter to court and the court ruled that the government had no right to use Ms. Lau's tax return for the purpose of discipline and for the purpose of terminating her employment. That gave her the right to the damages that a public servant would have for being fired. She was fired for cause but she got damages for being fired for cause.
This change in the statute makes sure that people who have a special ability in the administration of income tax cannot use the tax system, their own tax system, to make money.
March 30, 1993

We have a situation in which disciplinary action is required and the tax return of an employee is relevant to that disciplinary action, and only to that extent can the tax return be used. The guidelines will specifically and in detail control that use.
It seems to me, and I am sure to other people here as taxpayers, that people who are employees of Revenue Canada and are in the business of examining tax returns and organizing the tax system have specialized knowledge and inside information in terms of how things work.
Therefore it is important, if we are going to make sure the system is fair and honest for taxpayers, that those persons who are hired for that specific purpose know that their own returns can be used should they play games with the system and benefit themselves through information they have gathered as a result of their employment with Revenue Canada.
One could say that we could fire her, and Ms. Lau certainly did get fired, but the question really is whether this is a dismissal with cause or a dismissal subject to damage. It is the government's view that when people are deceitful and dishonest in Revenue Canada and it is necessary to use their tax information to prove that deceit and dishonesty that they should not be able to hide behind the privacy of their tax returns so that then-deceit and dishonesty cannot be legally shown and that deceit and dishonesty becomes a matter of employee discipline.
I think any fair-minded person would find that to be a fair statement and I suggest that the amendment is necessary. It came forward like this because we were not prepared to pass the bill and that section without the information and undertakings from the privacy commissioner. We now have those. We are now prepared to put the section before the House.
Therefore members on the government side in the committee deliberately did not vote on that clause when the clause was put by the chairman and consequently the clause did not pass.
Members of the committee did it that way because the most convenient way of doing the amendment, changing it and handling it was by not passing the clause at committee and reintroducing it at report stage so that it
Government Orders
could be passed. That was the clean, easy and neat way of doing it.
Everyone who was at the committee that evening knew that was going to happen. There is no deceit or misrepresentation here. It was perfectly obvious to everyone who was there exactly what we were doing. Otherwise we would have introduced detailed amendments at committee in connection with the particular clause before us. We did not do that simply because the cleanest, easiest and neatest way of handling the matter was to reintroduce the clause at report stage and put it to the House.
That is why it is before the House now. It was a neat, clean way of handling the matter and it would have been introduced in part form or altered form had the privacy commissioner not reported as he had. When he reported as he had the only proper and effective way of bringing this matter back to the House was to reintroduce the entire clause the way it was when the bill was first brought before the House at second reading.
That is the reason for it and that is why this amendment should pass.

Mr. Speaker, I was not at the committee and I have listened attentively to the member for Mississauga South. I do not want to debate his point on what happened technically to the clauses of the bill. I want to deal with the substance of what we are involved with here, and I am personally opposed to this.
To have a situation where-and it does not matter that we are putting the onus on the fact that they are Revenue Canada employees-managers or supervisors, by a law of the land, are allowed to have access to a person's tax return is obscene. If there is a suspicion by a manager that the employee is breaking the law then lay the charge. Simply lay the charge.
We all know that from time to time because of the nature of human beings there could be a moment of frustration or tension in which someone could use the tax system in a way that would not be just. They could use that tax system outside the actual basic law of treating someone fairly. They could use this as a way of harassment.
I do not think this is right in any way, shape or form.
I want to go back to the remarks put forward by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance because he was quoting selectively from a letter that was

March 30, 1993
Government Orders
written by the privacy commissioner of Canada to the deputy minister of revenue, Mr. Pierre Gravelle. I want to read the entire letter because when I read it I think members will see that this is not a case in which the privacy commissioner is completely satisfied with what is going on here.
It says: "Dear Mr. Gravelle: Thank you for your letter of this date", this is March 23, "regarding the proposed amendments to the Income Ikx Act and the Excise Tax Act and the concerns we expressed about them in my letter to you March 18. Let me say at the outset that I was gratified both by the tone and the substance of your letter. In the case of the former by your ready acknowledgement of the privacy interest in these matters, and in the latter by your proposal for a consultative process to develop proper privacy safeguards in disciplinary actions.
You noted that I did not disagree with the proposition that you have a right, indeed a duty, to ensure a high degree of employee integrity and particularly to satisfy yourself that no employee uses insider information for personal benefit. I am sure every Canadian supports that objective.
My concerns lie with the potential abuse. I suggested as a possible approach the establishment of stringent criteria for the examination of employee files for disciplinary purposes such as defining conditions of reasonable cause. It was satisfying, therefore, to learn that you already are in the process of developing guidelines with my office and other interested parties. I welcome this proposal, confident that together we can work out a satisfactory regime that protects privacy rights of employees.
Finally, let me acknowledge with pleasure that your interpretation of the "made language in the amendment to section 241" is the same as our own. Namely, that it is intended to enable Revenue Canada officials to carry out their duties under the Privacy Act.
I presume that your officials will soon be in touch with my office to initiate discussions on the guidelines mentioned above."
What we have here today is yet another example of this government's total disrespect for the House of
Commons. It is another example where this government with its majority and its lean, mean machine approach to governing this country is trying to slide through an amendment that would give the management of Revenue Canada the right to look at their employees' tax returns.
There is not a person in this country who would support that kind of treatment. There is not a businessman or businesswoman in this country who would support an initiative where the boss can look or can get access to a person's tax returns. Once something like this is put into law with Revenue Canada where does it go?
One could use the same logic and apply it to judges, departments that give out grants for industry and to every public servant. Every public servant in this country is in a position of trust. Every one of us in this House of Commons is in a position of trust. If I am doing something wrong then someone can lay a charge against me or the employer or whoever it is can lay a charge against any public servant. However, to use the legislative process of the House of Commons of Canada to try and slide through just this little amendment so that the management of Revenue Canada could look at their employees' tax returns is totally and utterly wrong.
Something else bothers me about this as well. We had the deputy minister of Revenue Canada in the public accounts committee last week. He is a great public servant and a man who is dedicated to his job.
I want to say that I was so shocked to find out that the Department of Revenue has done no cost-benefit analysis on the GST. It has done no analysis. We know that the revenue of the GST is approximately $30 billion. We know that it put out this number of $15 billion after the social credits and the operating costs such as the GST police and so on. There is a net of $15 billion.
It has no figure for what, for example, the restaurant sector in Canada was bringing into the national Treasury pre-GST and post-GST. It has no idea how the GST has affected tourism pre-GST and post-GST. Tourism employs almost 12 per cent of the nation's work force. The tourism receipts in this country are down by almost 35 per cent. One cannot find a tourism operator in this country who will not say that the GST has caused the damage.

March 30, 1993

That, in the opinion of this House, the government should
incorporate the following national objectives in all of its child care
initiatives:
1.	child care services should be licensed and regulated so that they apply the highest standards consistent with current knowledge of early childhood development;
2.	cost should not be a barrier to access to child care services;
3.	child care services should be universally accessible, irrespective of a person's income, employment status or geographic location;
4.	child care services should be comprehensive enough to offer services for infants, pre-schoolers, school-age children, and children with special needs, and be culturally sensitive;
5.	child care services should be flexible enough to accommodate the demand for full-time, part-time, seasonal, shift and occasional services;
6.	child care services should be operated on a non-profit basis.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I rise today to call for a national child care program which is accessible, affordable, comprehensive, culturally sensitive, of good quality, flexible and non-profit. Yes, that is a tall order, but it is an essential goal.
Many may lead us to believe that such a program is impossible but that does not explain how a number of European countries have achieved comprehensive, publicly funded national child care programs, some of which even include allowances for homemakers who raise small children full time.
Unlike most other developed affluent nations, Canada does not have a system of child care. Child care in Canada has developed in a haphazard manner driven by market forces.
Child care is a women's rights issue. The royal commission on equality and employment reported in 1984 that child care is the ramp that provides equal access to the work force for mothers.
Private Members' Business
In our society women are primarily responsible for child-rearing. This has resulted in the incredible poverty of older women who do not have pensions built up in their own name. It has also resulted in inequality between women and men workers. Our society must come to terms with blending work and family responsibilities in a way that does not penalize either the mother at home or the mother in the paid work force.
In 1990 Canada signed the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Child care is recognized in that convention as a significant children's rights issue. Every child has the right to adequate care either by a parent or by another caregiver.
France has an extensive and well-funded system of child care and women's equality is not used to justify it. They consider what is best for the children. Child care is a family issue. It should be there for parents who want or need to do paid work and to provide respite care for those at home who are child care workers 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
The Vanier Institute for the Family estimates that 1.3 million Canadian children are in need of child care. Yet there are only 300,000 licensed child care spaces in the entire country.
Child care is a social policy issue. Child care is a way to identify and to help abused children and to provide educational and other resources and opportunities for poor children that their parents are not able to afford.
Child care is an economic issue. It is an investment in a skilled and educated work force. It is about time government and employers realized that the majority of workers are parents and that the future workers and citizens may now be growing up with inadequate care that will have a major and long lasting impact on the future of our country.
Child care is an important issue, one which this government and the Liberals when in power have chosen to ignore. Even during these times of economic hardship the New Democrat governments in both British Columbia and Ontario have invested in the creation of new licensed child care spaces.
Canadian families have changed. Children are being raised in smaller families. This means fewer siblings and fewer aunts and uncles to care for children. Families are more mobile. Over 16 per cent of the Canadian population are immigrants. This means that parents and

March 30, 1993
Private Members' Business
children may not live in the same city as their grandparents and other family members, or they may have no extended families or strong networks of people who can care for their children while they financially support them.
Before the 1980s the paid labour force participation rates for mothers of pre-school children were lower than that for all other women. Now the rate for mothers of pre-schoolers has surpassed the paid labour force participation rate of all women.
The 1992 Canadian national child care study found that over half the families with pre-school children were dual earner couples or employed sole support parents.
It is harder to make ends meet these days and it is becoming impossible to raise a family on one income. Wages have not kept pace with inflation. Taxes have increased while services have been cut. The number of women raising children on their own has risen, both due to divorce and to the fact that many young, unmarried mothers choose to raise their children themselves.
I want to go through each point of my motion. First, child care must be of good quality. Child development research shows that the quality of care children receive has a profound effect on their future development. Some unregulated, informal or private arrangements may suit all parties; for instance, sometimes a grandmother who cares for her grandchildren while her daughter or son is in the paid work force. Sometimes for some families that works and it is a positive arrangement. She may be a good, experienced caregiver who has a lot of love and wisdom to share.
We have all heard the horror stories of other types of unlicensed care such as the alleged sexual abuse ring, run from an unlicensed, unregulated child care centre in Martensville, Saskatchewan. Abuse can also be a problem in unregulated care provided by friends or relatives.
A child is most likely to be abused by someone they know, by a friend, a family friend or a relative, than by anyone else. We must ensure that all Canadian children are being cared for in conditions which do not hurt their health, imperil their safety or close their minds. That means good staff-child ratios so that caregivers can interact frequently with each individual child. It means
fair wages, benefits and working conditions for child care workers so they do not bum out and a child can count on having the same caregiver for a period of several years. It means a physical environment which is safe and pleasant where kids can get fresh air. It means training in early childhood education for caregivers so they can structure programs appropriate for children's developmental levels.
When compared to France, Denmark, Sweden or Italy, Canadian child care is substandard on many counts and particularly deficient in staff training requirements. Not only must we have standards for care of our most important resource, our children, but those standards must be enforced.
Second, child care must be affordable. Since 1966 child care has been funded through the Canada Assistance Plan which is essentially a welfare program. The government has talked about giving parents choices, but currently many parents have no choice. They do not qualify for a subsidy, but cannot afford the full fees for care. Child care costs can take up almost all or a majority of a woman's yearly salary. A family with a pre-school child and one school age child can pay up to $12,000 a year for child care costs alone. It means a woman can end up working for $5,000, $6,000 or $7,000 a year after she has paid her child care costs.
The crying shame of this is that there are empty child care spaces out there that no one can afford and yet the line for subsidized child care spaces can be over a year long. That is a year when a parent must stay out of the paid work force or on welfare. Because of the shortage and ineligibility of many families for subsidized regulated spaces, many families are forced to turn to informal arrangements which can be unstable and for which they may not be able to get receipts to deduct on their income tax. Studies have found that unregulated arrangements have a high turnover rate which means the child is shunted about to a different caregiver every few months. People must have the option of affordable licensed child care.
Third, child care must be accessible regardless of income, employment status or geographic location. In Canada today, child care is simply not available in many rural areas, while both parents may be busy working on a farm or one is working in town while the other is working on the farm. Licensed child care is not accessible in Canada. Many families do not qualify for a subsidy and
March 30, 1993

yet cannot afford the enormous costs of child care. The gap between the availability of licensed child care and the number of mothers in the paid labour force has been widening over the past decade until it has become a huge gulf. By 1990 there were 500,000 more children under 13 with a mother in the paid labour force for whom there was no more regulated child care than there was in 1983.
Fourth, child care must be comprehensive, culturally sensitive and be able to deal with special needs. Cultural sensitivity, training and screening should be a part of staff training and hiring. No child should go to child care and come out of that child care centre with a lack of self-esteem.
Aboriginal communities face a particular challenge in terms of instilling knowledge and respect of traditional language, customs, values and spirituality. Aboriginal child care must be controlled by aboriginal communities.
Fifth, child care must be flexible enough so that it can be used on a full, part-time or occasional basis or seasonally or by shift workers.
I had three children in two years. I know what it is like to be at home in a low income, one income family trying to deal with the needs of three very small children, one of whom was critically ill. Parents who are in that position must have the availability of respite so that they can have care for their children and continue to have their young children socially interact with other children and move out of their own home environment for the health of both the parents and the children.
The Canadian national child care study reported last year that 55 per cent of parents with paid employment did not have a standard work schedule, that is Monday to Friday with no evening or weekend work. Yet most child care centres are only open from 8 a.m. to 6 p.m. or fewer hours. What care is there for children whose parents must work shift work? The need for flexible child care cannot be underestimated.
Why should taxpayers be paying good money for a child care centre's owner's profit rather than putting it directly into good nutrition and educational resources for children? There is a body of research that shows that commercial child care is on average of poorer quality than non-profit child care in the areas of child-staff
Private Members' Business
ratios, staff training, staff turnover and wages and benefits.
Far from giving parents an increased choice most parents trying to find child care have little choice but to take whatever is available unless they are wealthy enough to be able to shop around.
Choice in child care is a myth. Many choices for families are constrained by economics in more ways than one. Some women who are in the paid work force would prefer to be at home with their young children. Some women who are at home being supported by a partner or on welfare or living on small savings would prefer to be in the paid labour force but are constrained by the lack of child care.
They cannot go to school. They cannot go for training or retraining. They cannot look for work. They cannot accept work because there is no alternative care for their children.
We are living in Canada in a society with a declining birth rate. The 1986 task force on child care known as the Katie Cooke task force reported that people wrote to them saying that the lack of parental leave and child care had directly affected their own child bearing decisions not to become parents. Our society does not acknowledge the work women do in the home and consequently underpays child care workers as well.
Many child care workers particularly in regulated non-profit centres have degrees or certificates in early childhood education, experience, patience, responsibility and love and they are paid much less than many male workers in jobs that require less education and certainly less responsibility.
This government and the Liberals when in power have chosen to avoid the fact of the increased need for affordable child care until it has now reached crisis proportions.
As a society we will prosper or decline based on how we collectively care for our children and on what opportunities they have to learn and to grow and to receive adequate nutrition and care. These early years are very important in shaping the health and abilities of our future society. We cannot afford to overlook it or to shrug it off just because pre-schoolers cannot write letters to members of Parliament or lobby or demonstrate on the lawns of Parliament Hill.

March 30, 1993
Private Members' Business
In 1970 the Royal Commission on the Status of Women said of child care that we are faced with a situation that demands immediate action. That was in 1970. Twenty-three years later nothing at all has changed except that federal child care funding contributions to the Canada Assistance Plan have been capped which is choking the ability of the provinces to pay for child care and a Child Care Initiatives Fund was set up to fund research in innovative projects only to be cut back twice by millions of dollars.
The Family Allowance Program was a way that Canadian society recognized albeit in a small way the contribution made to society by those who raise children. That program was eliminated.
We are still faced with attitudes like that of the Conservative member of Parliament from Fraser Valley West who recently said that child care centres are: "little more than temporary orphanages".
The Liberals had 14 years to act and they did absolutely nothing except study the issue. The time to act has long passed. Let us join together now with parents and with communities to build a comprehensive child care system which also recognizes and values the contributions of parents in the home and a child care system on which to base our future as a nation.
Canadian women and Canadian families are in desperate need of licensed child care in this country. They are very tired and very fed up with a government that continues to spend money on big-ticket items like $5.8 billion for 50 helicopters at the expense of our nation's children.
