speakeroldname: Mrs. Suzanne Duplessis (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister for External Relations and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for External Relations; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, children are our future. Everyone agrees on that.
How we care for children today, the support they get from their parents, teachers, community leaders and governments, will determine the success of our society later on. Today's children will be tomorrow's grown-ups. They will have to look after their own children's education while earning a living and paying taxes.
The family unit has changed considerably over the years. Nowadays, both parents generally have jobs out of their home. It is an economic necessity.
Statistics Canada 1991 census shows that 69 per cent of women with young children are in the work force, compared to 49 per cent a decade ago, in 1981.
This represents a radical change which has a major impact on how our society is organized, from business hours to flexible work schedules, from our social support networks to the kind of child care services available.
Child care and education are two of the most important aspects of a nation's social policy. We are glad to live in a privileged country. In most cases our children are raised in a loving environment and they are well fed. They are provided with the support and social skills they need to grow into responsible adults. Parents should be proud of their children's successes and accomplishments in spite of the increasing pressures being put on modem families.
Not all children live under the same conditions however. Some children suffer from malnutrition and infantile diseases and do not receive quality health care. So, government has to give priority to these children and situations.
Faced with limited financial resources and competing demands, government was forced to make a choice in 1992. It had to chose between providing a national child care program, investing loads of money in a government plan aimed at all the children or working together with its partners to provide immediate assistance to those who are the most vulnerable. The government chose the latter.
Last year the Minister of National Health and Welfare announced Canada's action plan for children entitled Brighter Futures. This is an extensive strategy dealing with prevention, promotion, protection and community action for our children.
The new child benefit was a major feature of Brighter Futures. This benefit combined the family allowance, the child tax credit and the dependant child tax credit and increased payments by $2.1 billion over a five-year period.
March 30,1993

The child tax benefit also introduced a new earned-income supplement of up to $500 per family in recognition of the additional education costs faced by working families.
The child development initiative, Brighter Futures, is a $500-million program aimed particularly at vulnerable children. The federal government recognizes the importance of prevention. It wants to ensure that we look as early as possible after kids who are most likely to become sick or socially disadvantaged. The child development initiative is also targeted to parents at the community level. It enables them to acquire the necessary skills to raise their children even better.
Even though the government chose to direct additional money to children at risk rather than to child care services, it still supports the day care program. In fact, the amount spent by the federal government on day care services has quadrupled since 1984; it has gone from $250 million in 1984 to more than $1 billion last year. The government still supports this initiative.
For parents who work outside the home we have increased the maximum child care expense deduction on their income tax return starting with the current tax year. It goes up from $4,000 to $5,000 for each child under 7 or with special needs. For other eligible children the maximum deduction was raised from $2,000 to $3,000.
The government particularly looks after the need for child care services of parents taking training courses or trying to get off welfare. Employment and Immigration Canada makes payments totalling $75 million to trainees who need child care services.
Under the Canada Assistance Plan the federal government gives some $275 million a year to the provinces and territories to reserve day care spaces for low-income families.
Moreover, the federal government is a leader in national issues related to child care services through the Child Care Initiatives Fund. Since 1988 we have contributed more than $74 million for 468 national, regional and aboriginal projects.
All the programs which I mentioned, namely the child care expense deduction, the dependent allowances paid through CEIC training programs, the sharing of day care costs through the Canada Assistance Plan and the Child
Private Members' Business
Care Initiatives Fund still exist. In fact they have been improved or expanded since this government came to power.
It is inaccurate to say that our government spends less on daycare. We may not be spending enough according to some, and we may not be able to take on all these expenses.
Just like today's families, the government is facing new realities. We cannot ask our children to bear the debt resulting from new spending programs. There should be a return on each dollar that we spend today.
This is why we are concentrating our efforts on vulnerable children. And let us not forget that the federal government helps children and their families through many other programs on protecting and promoting health, family violence, Canada's Drug Strategy and the environment. The federal government also supports the provincial and territorial programs on health, welfare and social services through tax transfers such as Established Programs Financing and the Canada Assistance Plan.
In spite of what our critics might say this government has not abandoned the children of Canada, their families or the day care program. We continue to meet the needs of all children. However we have increased our resources to help the neediest children especially.
We want to help those children and to do so we must reach their parents. Young parents, especially single mothers, must gain the necessary basic skills to be able to feed their children properly. These mothers need help to get training so that they no longer depend on social assistance. It is a mistake to believe that single mothers who are on welfare do not want to be independent and take care of their children on their own.
That is why we stress how important it is to help families to become financially independent. To this end, we have added the earned income supplement to the child tax benefit in order to further help the working, low income families.
One must also recognize that governments cannot bear the entire responsibility. The time has come to demand that employers take more steps to meet the needs of their employees. An adequate social policy would be greatly appreciated by their workers and their

Mar
Private Members' Business
children and would be considered a good business decision.
We recognize that more must be done to allow all Canadians and in particular those who care for children to be able to be active members of society. We are committed to helping families escape the welfare merry-go-round.
It is probably the best hope we can give their children for a brighter future. These families will be able to state proudly that they can afford to support their children. In turn, their children will also feel that same pride and self-confidence which breeds autonomy. With the help of governments, social service agencies, communities and other partners this is the hope we can give all our children.

Mr. Speaker, it is my very great pleasure to support this motion this evening. Before I get into my support of this motion, I cannot allow the remarks of the hon. member for Louis-Hebert to go unremarked. Indeed they were remarkable. They were remarkable with the greatest of respect for the hon. member in their sheer tommy-rotness if there is such a word.
I heard the hon. member say that one of the reasons the government has not instituted a national child care program is because it would cost too much money. I quote the hon. member, translating freely, that we cannot ask our children to bear the burden of the debt of the expenditures that we authorize today.
That is a noble sentiment in some categories, but when one million Canadian children today are latch-key children, are without care for a significant portion of their day, I bet if we asked them, they might not mind so much paying off that debt somewhere down the road. That is the disgrace we face in this country today.
The second thing I want to say about all this is I want to hearken back to the royal commission on employment equity chaired by, as she is now, Madam Justice Rosalie Abella of the appeal division of the Supreme Court of Ontario. There was a sentence in that report which should be carved in stone on every public building in this
country. It perhaps should be carved in the stone of the heads of some of our colleagues. Those words are that child care is the bridge to employment equity.
I will go a step further because I suspect that most child care advocates, most women and most thinking men would agree with me that child care is the major bridge to gender equality in this country. Rightly or wrongly the major care givers for children are women. It is an unfortunate imbalance in the division of labour because both fathers and children would benefit greatly from more contact. That is a topic for another debate on another day.
In our society, indeed in western society and in the world society today, women are the care givers for children. If women are going to be able to take their full place in the labour force, if women are going to be able to work with a sense of security about their families, what great leap of logic does it take to say they must have adequate, accessible, affordable child care. I do not think you need an Einstein to set out that particular premise. We all know that is the case and the time has come to do something about it.
I realize my time is truncated. I have one minute so I will make the best of it. Mr. Speaker, I rise on a follow-up to a question I asked the Minister of National Defence on February 22. It was a question on peacekeeping of great concern to me.
The point I made in my question was the concern I had at that time, in consultation with other members of Parliament and as a result of some hearings in the Standing Committee on National Defence and Veterans Affairs, with the growing dependence of the Canadian forces on reserve forces. It was the result of what I believe was the overcommitment taken on by the government for peacekeeping around the world.
This is a very judgmental thing. I raised the question with the minister and she really did not answer it. She gave me a lecture on what the Canadian forces were doing and talked about the perspective of international affairs. I am going to quote here what she did say. She said:
In some instances we have deployed people where the United Nations has regarded our services of greater urgency than where they were at that particular time.
I was not sure what she meant by that. The minister went on to say that the Canadian forces were designed to meet domestic concerns and security concerns. I did not need the minister to tell me that. She continued:
When they are not needed on active deployment we make them available to the United Nations. This incurs costs to the Canadian people.
The minister was not entirely right there. My understanding is that there is a commitment and a contingency in the planning process to commit x number of peace-
Adjournment Debate
keepers. I know at one point in time that was roughly 2,000 when we had a larger force of soldiers by 4,000.
I realize that we are going to reduce our commitment to Cyprus and there is some juxtapositioning going on regarding the deployment of troops. However, there are two points I want to make in this late show.
It is now March 30 and I am seeing more and more experts saying that a 50 per cent ratio-in fact in the case of the battalion relieving in Croatia which is under way right now-we are looking at 55 per cent of the force being reservists. I have the greatest admiration, belief and faith in reserves. I have always been for the total force concept. In fact I was very much involved in making the naval reserves part of the over-all total force concept in the navy. However in this particular case 55 per cent is way out of whack.
It is not me saying that. I was saying it on February 22, but in the latter days of this month of March no less than four experts are saying that 50 per cent is too much. They are saying that we are endangering our peacekeepers and we are doing things that we should not be doing. A recognized expert says that 10 per cent is about right. Whether it is 10 per cent, 5 per cent or 20 per cent, the fact is that 50 per cent is too much.
We have 60,000 peacekeepers deployed in the world today. Canada has 4,800 and that represents 8 per cent. We make up one-half of 1 per cent of the world's population. I think we are doing at least our share. One could argue we are doing more than our share.
My talking in the late show is not going to really achieve very much. I will get a response from the parliamentary secretary and then we will get on with other business. However, before we have any further commitment to United Nations peacekeeping operations, as they are not necessarily the old, low intensity peacekeeping operations that we knew in the past, we need to have a debate in this House. That is the point I was making to the minister and she missed it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the Minister of National Defence, I would like to thank the hon. member for his question. As

March 30, 1993

Although important, our participation in United Nations peacekeeping operations in only one aspect of our defence policy. It is an aspect of our activities that is a source of great pride among members of the Canadian Forces and contributes every day to increasing Canada's international reputation as one of the greatest supporters of the United Nations.
The Canadian forces now have sufficient resources to meet their obligations in peacekeeping operations. Although we are near our limit, the Canadian forces are still able to do their duty with the same professionalism and dedication that we have witnessed over the past 40 years.
Canadian troops are deployed in United Nations peacekeeping operations with the same care and attention that we have always shown in deploying our troops, whether in exercises or operations abroad. Canada maintains command of all its forces that are deployed in United Nations peacekeeping missions.
The question of our troops' safety was also raised, particularly concerning the type of armored vehicles that we use in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to seek answers from the Minister of Finance regarding what would appear to be a serious injustice done by his office and officials to the Sovereign Life Insurance Company, its employees and policy holders.
March 30, 1993

Last February 5,1 asked the minister to tell the House precisely why the government had shut down the only federally regulated life insurance company in Calgary. Perhaps the parliamentary secretary will respond today. The junior minister certainly did not adequately answer then.
It would appear the minister's seizure of Sovereign Life on December 21, 1992 was based on grossly defective and irresponsible information his office received from the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, OSFI.
The Minister of State for Finance was present on November 30, 1992 when the company asked for an 80-day extension to produce audited 1992 financial statements and an unqualified actuarial opinion. He also had an independent actuarial opinion that the extension was warranted.
The actuaries, both highly respected individuals and one of whom used to be a member of this House, concluded as follows: If Sovereign were seized and liquidated, thousands of policy holders would incur losses; the company's position at the end of 1992 would be more favourable than indicated in the provisional actuarial opinion of November 11, 1992; and the only signed opinion the minister had before him on December 13, 1992 was that by the OSFI's own solvency test, "the MCCSR", Sovereign would be solvent at the end of 1992 and would improve its position during 1993. The OSFI significantly refused to provide any signed actuarial opinion.
The December 31, 1991 financial statement of Sovereign contained a $40 million error which was later adjusted in Sovereign's favour. At all times there were excess resources of $52 million. Does the minister or government dispute this? I think not.
The finance minister was not even present when Alan Graham, the former owner of Sovereign Life, made his presentation to the junior finance minister.
Despite a requirement of the relevant legislation, the senior finance minister subsequently ordered the company to be seized. It is the first time in 100 years a federal life insurance company had been brought down by Ottawa.
Adjournment Debate
The seizure will affect about 240,000 Sovereign policy holders, 1,000 Sovereign brokers, 250 head office employees in Calgary, 300 in-house Sovereign agents. It will also affect about $810 million in company assets.
The minister's decision to take Sovereign over was appealed to the federal government on December 23. Has the government failed to file a response because there is no real response?
Sovereign was supposed to have its day in court today, but when an Alberta Court of Queen's Bench justice ruled to delay the legal action of the federal government until next September, Mr. Graham reportedly decided to turn to the Federal Court.
Why did this government attempt to have dismissed the shareholder action in Calgary seeking the right to represent Sovereign Life in the Federal Court in pursuing a claim for damages against the government agencies involved? Is this government afraid of the truth on this matter?
Finally, whatever might transpire in the courts will not alter the fact that the government has made another grave public policy error. What does the government intend to do to minimize the damage this grossly irresponsible action has done to a major financial institution in western Canada?

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel R. TVemblay (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to answer the question asked on February 5 by the hon. member for Edmonton Southeast on the Sovereign Life Insurance Company.
On December 21, 1992 the Finance minister, after a report by the Superintendent of Financial Institutions to the effect that the assets of Sovereign were not adequate to properly protect its policy holders and creditors and, after the company was given the opportunity to state its case, ordered that the Sovereign Life Insurance Company be placed under the control of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions.
The minister and the Superintendent acted promptly to preserve the assets and the residual value of this company for the benefit of policy holders. They both acted in accordance with their responsibilities under the Insurance Companies Act.

March 30, 1993
Adjournment Debate
Before deciding to shut down the company considerable efforts were put into finding an investor who would inject money to allow the company to carry on and provide coverage to all its clients.
Unfortunately no one made a firm commitment to invest a larger amount of money and the Canadian Life and Health Insurance Compensation Corporation, an organization similar to CDIC but financed by the industry, did not take part in an assistance program to make the merger easier. The main responsibility of the minister and the superintendent is to protect those who entrusted Canadian financial institutions with their assets.
The Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions regulates about 175 life insurance companies. It has been doing so for a long time.
As far as the Sovereign Life Insurance Company is concerned, the company's finances were assessed by the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions and its report did not match assessments made by the company itself. After going through the accounting records potential buyers were not as optimistic about the financial situation of the company. That would explain why no other prospective buyer was to be found.

Mr. Speaker, on February 11, when we were debating the Unemployment Insurance bill, the hon. member for Laval-Est said, and I quote: "I have reported some myself and I am still alive. I am fed up with paying taxes and giving to the poor. I want everybody to be rich because if I am surrounded by poor people, some day they will steal from me or kill me."
That was a remark, as I said before, supposedly made by the hon. member for Laval-Est.
He made another remark, speaking in English, and I quote:

"It is the cheapest way and it is the best way to police a system. We can keep it confidential. You do not have to identify yourself. You just report to the government a neighbour or a friend".
My purpose on that particular day was to try to determine whether or not those particular quotations attributed to that particular member of Parliament were in fact correct, whether or not they were in line with the minister's thinking and whether or not they were government policy.
It just so happened that for some reason the Speaker of the day felt that perhaps these should not be read into the record. I felt rather badly about it because certainly I had taken them from public documents. I was not charging the member. I was simply saying it was attributed to that member. In fact the member could have risen if they were incorrect and dissociated himself from them.
In the ensuing debate the minister who was a little hot under the collar indicated and tried to denigrate the questions by suggesting that I had prepared them ahead of time and they had not heard that he had decided not to have that particular 1-800 line, often referred to as a snitch-line.
My subsequent question to that minister was, in spite of the fact that he had decided not to have that particular 1-800 number, would it be the policy of this government to encourage people to report others.
I think you can agree, Mr. Speaker, that there are some people who would take that responsibility much more seriously than others. There are some individuals unfortunately who would probably do so with a certain amount of glee. I do not like the notion of trying to encourage people from reporting others, particularly when they do not have to identify themselves.
It is quite easy to pick up the telephone and make any kind of charge, particularly when you do not have to identify yourself.

We know that this bill has now been passed by the government. I hope the government will not ask people to report their neighbours or their next of kin. I think it would be useless and dangerous to encourage such a policy since there would be no need to identify yourself and it would be so easy to do it.
[English ]
Therefore I await the response of the parliamentary secretary with a certain amount of anticipation. I am pleased that I have an opportunity to correct the record
March 30, 1993

and I am anxious to find out what the government has to say about this particular matter.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is unfortunate that my hon. friend would bring forward and try to resurrect an issue that was a false issue in the first place because the minister at no time ever considered a so-called snitchline. That should have put an end to all debate in this House of Commons about it.
I would like to take advantage of this opportunity to inform my hon. friend about some of this government's activities to get Canadians back to work.
In 1992-93 Employment and Immigration Canada is investing $3.55 billion in providing training and employment assistance for over 900,000 Canadians. For 1993-94 we are increasing the UI developmental uses budget by another $260 million, bringing it to a total of $2.21 billion and EIC's over-all expenditures on training and employment assistance to $3.8 billion. With that $3.8 billion we will be providing assistance to over one million Canadians.
In 1993 some 326,000 Canadians will receive skills training through UI developmental uses, $110 million in self-employment assistance will encourage participants in their efforts toward greater self-sufficiency, and $15 million will go to assist workers to move to other localities where they have found jobs. Over 11,000 Canadians will be assisted under these programs.
The $120 million that is now budgeted for UI job creation will assist over 31,000 unemployed workers to get back into the work force by maintaining and enhancing their skills, and $130 million in work sharing assistance will allow employers and workers to jointly manage periods of production slow-down without reverting to lay-offs. Some 160,000 Canadians will participate in this initiative.

Mr. Speaker, tonight this brief exchange is on the North American free trade agreement, and in particular on the question of the environmental agreement that will be required if this trade agreement is to eventually become a reality.
Adjournment Debate
I would like to refer more specifically to the exchange in Question Period on March 18 when I raised with the minister the question of the role of the North American commission on the environment. I urged him during that exchange to let us know whether this commission, which would be in charge of environmental management, the environment being the basis of our economy, would have powers to enforce environmental laws and standards.
The minister was visibly preoccupied with the question of sovereignty and the violation of sovereignty should such a commission become involved with enforcement of environmental standards, for instance. As often happens in exchanges in Question Period we got nowhere. It was like two trains passing by in the middle of the night.
Therefore I would like to put forward some thoughts and some possible suggestions concerning this North American commission on the environment. I will draw heavily in the two minutes available from a colloquium sponsored by the North American institute in Santa Fe, New Mexico, from February 12 to February 14 of this year.
In this report, which resulted from this symposium on the North American environment, there are a set of recommendations, the examination of which by this government would certainly be worth while. They ought to be the object of discussions by those officials who will be in charge of further deliberations in Washington with the Americans and the Mexicans.
The North American commission on the environment could play a role in regularly reviewing environmental programs of the three countries with the specific goal of strengthening and harmonizing upward environmental laws and enforcement in the three countries.
The same commission could have an oversight function with the help of the environmental ministries of the three governments and could also report annually to the three governments and the public.
The proposed commission should form part of the North American free trade agreement dispute resolution process when environmental questions are raised. This same commission should be institutionalized through

March 30, 1993
Adjournment Debate
appropriate mechanisms and I will not go into the details of the mechanism because of lack of time.
This commission under the mandate given it by the three governments should receive references from the government to investigate and report on matters of trilateral concern. This commission in its environmental monitoring role should provide particular attention to migratory species and the protection of trans-boundary natural resources.
This is where we probably differ. This commission ought to go beyond performing a monitoring role and should have some teeth.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Shields (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I would like to repeat the question that was put before the minister and it was as follows: "Will the government give its unqualified commitment that the proposed North American commission on the environment will have powers to enforce environmental laws and standards?"
The functions of the commission are still being negotiated among the three governments. At the first trilateral meeting Canada put forward proposals developed following consultations with the provincial governments, non-governmental organizations and other private-sector interests including business and labour representatives.
Our starting point is that the North American commission on the environment should strengthen trilateral co-operation and development and the enforcement of regulations to protect the environment. Our aim is to encourage the upward harmonization of environmental regulations and standards.
We also want to be confident that our respective domestic and environmental laws and regulations will be eniorced. We seek a commission that respects the sovereignty of each party and at the same time provides strong assurances that domestic environmental law will be enforced and even improved over time.
The use of trade sanctions to enforce environmental standards would be a mistake. The use of trade sanctions could seriously harm vital Canadian trade and economic interests.

Mr. Speaker, on December 7 of last year I put a question to the Minister of Agriculture regarding the cut in subsidies to Canadian dairy farmers. That cut, although not very large, justifiably angered many dairy farmers who, over the last few years, were very concerned about the Dunkel report and the GATT negotiations. This cut just added to their anxiety, and I can understand that.
Dairy farmers are very much aware that the quota system, which is fundamental to the Canadian dairy industry, is being eroded. Not only are subsidies reduced but we can now read in various articles that a new way of measuring quotas is being sought.
Naturally quotas are extremely important and they really determine the value of a farm. The land and the buildings certainly have value, but without quotas that value is greatly reduced. Faced with this cut in subsidies the farmers would like to have an answer to this crucial question: Is the government still committed to defend and maintain milk production quotas? It is essential that dairy producers be assured that the quota system will never be jeopardized and will be kept intact. Dairy producers have to be guaranteed a certain price and not be faced every year with a cut in subsidies. We know that our dairy industry is very efficient; notwithstanding its critics, proof of that was given in the past.
In brief, the question dairy producers are asking is whether the quota system which has now existed for years and years in Canada will remain untouched? Moreover, they do not want any change without being thoroughly consulted.

speakeroldname: Mr. Marcel R. Tremblay (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance; Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to respond to a question that was raised in this House on December 7 by the hon. member for Gatineau-La Lievre concerning the cut in the subsidies to the dairy industry.
Mr. Speaker, you will recall that in his economic statement of December 2, 1992 the Minister of Finance stated that as part of the government effort to control the budget deficit the processed milk subsidy would be cut by 10 per cent in the next two fiscal years.
March 30, 1993

It is important to mention that there are two markets for milk in Canada: the market for milk (milk and fresh cream) and the market for industrial milk, which is used to make milk products such as butter, cheese and yoghourt. Producers get direct support payments of $ 6.03 per hectoliter of milk only for the deliveries of milk and cream required to meet domestic needs. Since the majority of producers make both fluid milk and industrial milk the cut in the federal subsidy does not affect their total production in most cases.
In times of budget restraints, tough decisions must sometimes be made. The subsidy cut would result in a decrease in revenues of no more than 60 cents per hectoliter of milk, or about 1.2 per cent. That is what the Minister of State for Agriculture answered when asked that question on December 7, 1992.
Even after this reduction, industrial milk producers will continue to receive over $200 million a year in subsidies from our government for their production of industrial milk.
How the subsidy cut will be implemented remains to be determined. It could be done in two different ways.
Adjournment Debate
The first possibility is to reduce the producer's target income by an amount equal to the subsidy cut. Producers would absorb the reduction and the prices of dairy products would remain unchanged.
The alternative is to increase support prices for butter and/or skim milk powder, which means that consumers would pay for the reduced subsidy. The producers' income per hectolitre would therefore remain unchanged, but the resulting price increase could have a slightly negative effect on demand for dairy products.
A third possibility would be to have producers and consumers share the impact of the lower subsidy.
I see that my time has expired. I would have liked to talk about quotas but time does not allow it.
